[SPEAKER_02]
Well thank you Rex for having me. Thank you all for being here this morning. Hopefully you'll find this useful. I don't use PowerPoint because it's boring, so I'm not going to do that. I'd rather take time to hear from you all and be able to answer some questions. So I thought I'd give a little overview of CFSI, our work in this space. I've also been asked to talk a little bit about what's going on in the regulatory space and how that might impact a number of fintech companies and then we're going to do a little bit of Q &A. So in terms of CFSI, as Rex said, we started in 2004 with a grant from the Ford Foundation and Jen Tescher who started our organization. The main question that they were looking at at the time was how many people in this country are unbanked? So it really questions around access. And at the time, I mean, people didn't know the answer to that and many people didn't even use the terms like unbanked or underbanked or underserved. Now it's kind of part of the parlance, but that was something we worked on for probably five or six years. And now we live in a world where the FDIC, as they just issued their new study, they look at this on an annual basis. But this was really important to think about, do people have access to the services and products they need in order to live their best financial lives? Over the next five to six years, really a lot of work began around innovation. Obviously, innovation is in the name, the Consumer Financial Services Center for Financial Services Innovation. And a big part of that was we had a fund at the time, which is now Core Capital, which you may know, some of you may know Arian, who's here in San Francisco and Los Angeles. But at that point, we spun that out. And JP Morgan later came along and said, we would like to fund the Financial Solutions Lab. The idea being, how can we help fund and support and accelerate companies that are interested in providing these types of products and services to consumers? And I think even back then, was still a little bit around inclusion. Maria, who's here on our team, she was here at the very, very beginning, so she could talk more about that. But we, over the last five years, have morphed more to looking at financial health. So that really gets to not the question of whether, do you have a product or service, but does it actually provide the support that you need in order for you to go out and live your best financial life? This is a much more complicated question to answer than, do you have a bank account? Or do you have an account? Do you have a prepaid card? Do you have a mortgage? This question of, how do we know that someone is living a more financially healthy life? This isn't point of the talk today, but I would note that in the next few weeks, you will see us coming out with a national survey that we'll be doing on an annual basis called The Pulse. Part of it is we want to get people to move away from talking about just GDP and unemployment and all these other measures of the overall economy's health, but are consumers being able to access products? Do they feel more or less stressed about their financial lives? How much leverage do they have? And so we've done a lot of work there, and we hope that that becomes part of the way we think about all the stuff that everyone in this room works on, which is what are we doing to address that for all Americans? As many of you know, over 80 % of Americans do experience some kind of financial distress in a given year, and almost half of Americans have less than $400 available to them in the event of an emergency. Just think about that for a minute. That is a very, very precarious situation for people to live in, and the more we understand what are the causes of that and what are the indicators of that would be quite valuable. So that's sort of where we've moved from inclusion and access to a world of financial health. And as part of that, the lab is a place where we express that through both capital and services we provide to firms that are looking to solve this. And with our next cohort, which will be announced in January, to reinforce this idea, we have an academic researcher from Wash U who's helping us to track over the coming two years whether the work that the firm, that these individual companies and firms are doing, is actually having an impact on consumers, who in this case are employees, because these firms will be providing services to employees through an employer. These are very important questions. These are not necessarily questions that the private market is set up to answer, because it's not necessarily your job when you're the investor to always think about this. I think it's a fundamental responsibility, but that isn't the system we live in. And so we are trying to move more and more toward that. Some people ask me, well, you know, I'm not really aware of financial health, or how would you help me think about these issues. This came up at my table earlier this morning, but I would encourage any of you who haven't read the Financial Diaries, which is a project that we did with Citibank, that that would be the best place to start. And I'm not just here to plug a book by us, but it is quite unique compared to anything else out there. We took families and we followed every single dollar that went in and out of their house for a whole year. And as many of you who work in communities that are low to moderate income, you know that the financial lives of people as you move down the income spectrum become increasingly complex, very, very difficult to attract, very difficult to understand the choices that people have to make, the risks that they face, because as you go up the income spectrum, the risks that we all face start to narrow and become quite uniform. And so I would encourage each of you, depending on what products you're working on, to think about how can you get closer to that understanding. And as part of that, one of the things I would just note that we're working on, is thinking more about how do we incubate companies. And one way to do that is to think about how do we get closer to the consumer. So one of the one of the ideas is do you co -locate an incubator at a place that has a large number of consumers who get direct services. So no decisions have been made, but one of the hypothesis we're working on at the moment, and we'll discuss tomorrow, Adam and Maria and I, is, for example, in DC where I live, the food bank serves half a million different people a year, which is on its face something that should be kind of shocking, since I live in a metro area that's only six million people. But that's a place where you have people with very pertinent needs, the kinds of work we do, get you distribution, which by the way, any of you work on startups, as you know, distribution is like 150 % of the problem. Banks already have that, by the way. They might not be innovators, but they've got distribution down. So that's a place where we're trying to get closer to the consumer and see if we could be building products and building companies in the very heart of where people are living their lives. So that's one thing I would note. Lastly, I would just say, you know, we would love to work with any and all of you in some form or fashion through both the Financial Solutions Lab and our broader innovation efforts. So we do work from pre -product all the way up to the largest banks in the world on these issues. We have a number of our network members who do this kind of measurement for both their employees and their customers. So I thought now I'd move on to some of the regulatory questions that have been asked to at least pose, and then I will stop and we'll have a little Q &A. So in the last two years, some of you might have noticed that politics has changed a little bit. So that's probably affecting your businesses. Some people, affects your mental health, but it also affects your businesses. So there's a couple of things I would point out. I don't think any of are inherently positive or negative. They're just different, and we don't know how some of them will turn out. For two things, as many of you know, there's now a FinTech charter application available through the OCC, which is the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which has got to be the most un -useful name for an agency. I don't think most people know what a Comptroller is. They kind of know what the currency is, but they don't know what the Comptroller would do with that currency. But anyway, they're the place that you go for all of the new types of chartering. At the moment, there are people who have applied, but no one's been accepted. We could talk more about why my personal view is that that is not going to succeed, and I would not expect anyone to actually make it through that process and actually accept the types of terms and conditions that would come with it. Second are de novo bank charters. So that is just applying to be a regular bank. And VARO money has gone through that process. You still have the FDIC, so good luck with that. That comes down to an insurance fund. They tend to be quite conservative. I used to be a deputy there. But VARO has shown that this can be done. Multiple firms have applied. A number of people pulled their applications for a number of reasons. I would say they're all quite different issues that they faced. But the de novo bank charter, it's very clear what you have, right? It's a bank. A bank comes with preemption. It comes with deposits. It comes with all kinds of things. Fintech charter is not clear what it comes with and what it doesn't come with. So we do see more activity happening on the de novo bank charter side. That's I would point out a couple of other big, big things. One is real time payments. So as many of you know, we're the only major – well, I wouldn't even say major developed country. I'd say one of the only countries in the world at this point that has a payment system that's quite this rigid and slow. So it can take up to three days to settle a check, which for low to moderate income consumers is an eternity. That's very problematic. But we have a system that is very, very slow. Many people, many of whom are in this city, have worked very hard to create workarounds so that people can move cash much more quickly. I was with the Boston Fed last week. The Fed is working very hard to push forward with real -time payments. In Fed years, that's probably 2021, 2022, but that will have a huge impact for consumers. I think a real -time payment system would be quite beneficial. However, it will be disruptive to a number of the business models that have been developed to try to create real -time payments. As someone who used to be a policymaker, I think there's a public good to having a real -time payment system. I think that that is better for everyone to build off of those rails as opposed to what we have today, but that could be quite disruptive. There will be fits and starts, and there will be people in the system who really want that and people who really don't want that. That is something that the Fed is committed to publicly now and has a Fed governor in Lael Brainerd who this is what she wants to work on. Lastly, I would talk a little bit about data. Not because data is the least important, but because it's the most complicated. But we seem to be entering a phase where the regulation of data and the use of data, the aggregation of data, who owns data, all of those questions are starting to come to the fore on the regulatory side. So, we are going through a cycle where the regulation of financial services seems to be waning. Not as quickly as I expected, but it is waning. We may be entering the first phase of regulation of data, because we really haven't had, other than some rules around privacy, around bank data, the way that data gets used today and who owns it and where it gets moved and how it gets supplemented with other data, it's not something people ever contemplated. I would just say in my visits to the Hill and with other regulators, this is very much on their minds about whether someone is a data fiduciary, whether someone owns data, who gets to decide when to turn data on and off to an aggregator. Does an aggregator need to have a series of bilateral agreements or should there be some templated system? Many of you in this room, I'm sure, face this problem every day, but it is something that is coming more to the fore. It is really complicated and our system of having very, very large banks, thousands upon thousands of small institutions and credit unions combined with a large number of non -bank financial institutions and then a number of non -regulated data providers makes this a difficult question to answer. And if you go to Washington and you ask who's in charge, who has a say, nobody and everybody. So it makes it hard to do the work, but it's something that I'm working on, we're working on at CFSI because this is an important question for us to be able to get toward innovation. So, I think with that, I'll just give a few concrete examples of where I think some of the regulatory changes will have real impact and then I'll stop. So the reason I stopped with data and real -time payments is I think those are the most pressing issues. At the end of the day, the bank charters and all that really get down to competitive advantages, access to capital, things that are very rudimentary to just running a business. On the data side, we saw with Plaid and JP Morgan having a bilateral agreement. We've seen a lot of small bilateral agreements from behind the scenes. It's my understanding that the Clearinghouse will be coming out with its proposal very, very soon. And so in 2019, there is going to be a lot of back and forth. And how some of these questions start getting settled really matter. So, one of the debates on the table is if you set up an API that allows you to pull data from a bank, if you're an aggregator or if you're providing a service to consumer, are there going to be requirements about what data you're allowed to pull or they must provide? So, for example, there are conversations on the table right now that would allow you to pull transaction data but would not allow you to pull price and fee data. As a former regulator, that's mind blowing to me because at the end of the day, if a customer doesn't know what they pay for the thing they just bought and they can't compare, that seems like that could be problematic. And not as effective as we all envision when many of us set out to do this work. So that is a debate that is on the table. Then second is are we going to have an API regime that can be rolled out to all these small institutions? So, for the large institutions, this is not that difficult. It's a pain, but JPMorgan has 50,000 IT employees. So, it could be done. As you go down the community banks, I don't know if anyone hears from Fiserv or FIS or Jack Henry, but the vast majority of banks in this country, actually their back office, their back -end IT is not theirs. They use a core processor. And so as a result, they don't really have the ability to make that decision themselves. And all of the core processors have different competitive interests about how they want to engage with APIs and with outside providers. And so those are going to become more and more pressing issues. And then I would say the other part of this is I increasingly hear various fintechs talk about they're gathering data that they don't need today, but they might need for some product they're going to offer in the future. As a former regulator, that is deeply concerning because certain types of data cannot be requested or used if you're providing something like a mortgage. There's certain types of information you can't have. There's information you can have to do for insurance, but you can't use it for a mortgage. In the old system, this problem didn't matter. This kind of cross -pollinization didn't matter because you had a mortgage division. They pulled in the data they needed. They underwrote it. They made a decision. But people are starting to envision where they're going to pivot and they pull in data. And it just concerns me that under another regulatory regime, that could be problematic for folks. And then lastly, with real -time payments, I think I already sort of spoke to this. It's pretty clear in a world where there's real -time payments, there's a lot of infrastructure that's been built to work around how broken the system is. And that could obviously have an impact on people who are in those businesses. And they'll have to think about how they need to prepare for a world where their underlying product doesn't have the same value because there should be or could be a public good that provides that. So with that, I'm going to stop so that we can get to more back and forth in Q &A. right. Thanks.

So they're investing at every stage. And they're a lot less price sensitive than other funds. So seed has held up, seed pricing has held up more than I would have expected. Now, the other thing is, even though valuations are down, round sizes are down, it still costs a lot of money to rent an apartment in San Francisco. And so it also costs a lot of money to hire an engineer. And that inflation has impacted everyone. So the price of hiring folks has stayed consistent. So you still need a certain amount of money to get your company off the ground. And that's what we're seeing. So what does the future look like? Well, I actually have no idea. I can tell you what today looks like. Today, I'd say like, in terms of pricing, we're seeing pre -seed rounds kind of return to the 2019 era. I'll say, and for us, we've done pre -seeds in the five to 10 range, seeds in the 10 to 20 or maybe a little bit higher for outstanding founders range. We're seeing series A's in the 30 to $70 million range. We're seeing series B's in the 100 to $150 million range. So, you know, things are down pretty significantly from where they were a year ago. I do think though, there will continue to be lots of capital available for great ideas and founders. But I do think, unfortunately, we're no longer the bell at the ball. Like people who changed their Twitter profile, the FinTech investor two years ago, then they changed it to Web3 investor. And today, they're just venture investor. So I think a little bit of the sheen has come off as we've seen, you know, the public markets fall in FinTech, we've seen it across the board. So I don't think we're going to get back to the multiples of 2021 anytime soon, which is very unfortunate for all of our portfolios. But I do think that there will be less competition out there. And there are lots of great folks in the market. So I think it's a great time, maybe as great a time as ever to buckle up and build a great sustainable business. And if you're doing that, I'd love to find you. So please talk to me. That's it.

[None]
He's did it. Yes. Totally. So much flattery. I'll take my payment later.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. And it's returned.

[SPEAKER_01]
My guests have been Seth Rosenberg, Shilmanat. Thank you so much for coming to the podcast.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thanks for having us. Cheers.

[SPEAKER_01]
If you're an early stage entrepreneur, we'd love to hear from you. Please hit us up at villageglobal.vc slash network catalyst. Bye.

[None]
Bye. Bye. Bye. Bye. Bye. Bye. Thank you.

[SPEAKER_01]
Looking for a guaranteed way to create content that resonates with your audience? Start a podcast. Interview your ideal clients and let them choose the topic of the interview. Because if your ideal clients care about the topic, there's a good chance the rest of your audience will care about it too. Learn more at sweetfishmedia.com.

[SPEAKER_03]
You're listening to B2B Growth, a daily podcast for B2B leaders. We've interviewed names you've probably heard before, like Gary Vaynerchuk and Simon Sinek, but you've probably never heard from the majority of our guests. That's because the bulk of our interviews aren't with professional speakers and authors. Most of our guests are in the trenches, leading sales and marketing teams. They're implementing strategy. They're experimenting with tactics. They're building the fastest growing B2B companies in the world. My name is James Carberry. I'm the founder of Sweetfish Media, a podcast agency for B2B brands. And I'm also one of the co -hosts of this show. When we're not interviewing sales and marketing leaders, you'll hear stories from behind the scenes of our own business. We'll share the ups and downs of our journey as we attempt to take over the world. Just kidding. Well, maybe. Let's get into the show.

[SPEAKER_04]
Welcome back to B2B Growth. I'm your host for today's episode, Nikki Ivey with Sweetfish Media. Guys, I've got with me today Ashish Dumbary, who is Vice President of Marketing at SkillJar. Ashish, how are you doing today?

[SPEAKER_00]
Nikki, thanks for having me. It's great to be on the show.

[SPEAKER_04]
Yeah, I'm excited. Guys, we're going to be talking about how education drives growth. that's both company growth and career growth. So I'm excited to really dig in. But before we do, before we get into all of that, Ashish, I'd love it if you would just give us a little bit of background on yourself and what you and the folks at SkillJar have been up to these days.

[SPEAKER_00]
Fantastic. Yes, so I run marketing here at SkillJar and SkillJar is the leading customer training platform. And what we do is help companies accelerate product adoption and increase retention. We work with companies like Tableau, Zendesk, Smartsheet, Cisco, and we help them deliver just beautiful customer experiences that are backed by data. Essentially, we give you all the tools that you need for customer training and enablement. And you can use those to onboard, engage, and retain your customers. So that's a little bit about SkillJar. We're based in Seattle. And I'm excited to have the conversation today.

[SPEAKER_04]
Yes, me too. I haven't had anybody that does exactly what you guys do on the show yet. So thanks for laying that out for us. I think it's great to be bringing something a little fresh to our listeners. And freshness and, like I said, like you mentioned, this idea of education and what you guys do is a little bit different than we're going to be talking about today. But there is a common threat, which is this idea that education drives growth. So give us a quick overview of what compelled you to write the piece that you wrote about this a while back and why you think this is so important.

[SPEAKER_00]
Absolutely. You know, in general, what I find is when you work at a startup, it's just a very fertile environment for you to grow your career. And a key driver of that is curiosity. If you're curious, that drives learning and that drives growth. A lot of growth in any company, it doesn't really matter how big the company is, happens in the cracks between departments. So this is where you don't really know who owns it. It could be owned by sales, by marketing, and by customer success. And if you find opportunities like that, you can shape your own role. You can shape the growth of the company. And that obviously drives growth for both the company and the individual. So I've been doing a lot of thinking on how best to do it. And, you know, a few things come to mind. This is, SkillJar is my fifth startup. So I've had the opportunity to observe what's worked for other people, what's worked for me, and identify some patterns that I'll speak to here. I don't think this is an exhaustive list, but these are just probably my top three or four observations. I'd say the number one thing you should always try to learn about is your customer. And this comes down to who are they, right? So this is personas, what type of companies are they in, what roles, what titles, but also what are the problems that they're trying to solve? And here, there's a particular framework that was developed by Clayton Christensen. You've probably heard of The Innovator's Dilemma, which is a very, really popular book that he wrote. There's an article that he wrote on this framework. It's really popular with product folks, and it's worth learning. Every marketer should get a good sense for it because it gives you an understanding of the problems that people are trying to solve. You know, that also then leads into the emotional landscape for your customers. Empathy is a marketing superpower. And I think you can think about human beings as fundamentally emotional beings that are really good at giving rational, logical answers for why they made a decision. But actually, what's driving the decision is a lot of emotions. And this is both positive emotions and negative emotions. So just having a sense for that landscape can be very powerful. This helps you figure out how you can uniquely help a customer. And also, what the stories that people are telling themselves, every human being has sort of navigates their life with stories, with each on a hero's journey of some sorts. So if you can get a sense for that for the prospect, you are functioning at a level that most companies are just not functioning at. And learning about that is super important. Some elements that help you learn that are obviously psychology and behavioral economics. Because there's a big difference in this view of customers or human beings as being purely rational beings. Reality tends to be a lot messier. We're not always rational. So the more you can learn about that, the more you can apply it in marketing. Daniel Kahneman has a fantastic book called Thinking Fast and Slow,

[None]
which

[SPEAKER_00]
gets into this. Richard Thaler has a really good book called Nudge that gets into this. There are any number of really good blog posts and blogs out there. Farnam Street, which is this blog that's based in Canada, is one of my favorites. And they have a podcast that's really good. So just some recommendations. You know, a couple of other things quickly. Marketing technology, if you're in marketing, there's been this Cambrian explosion of technology that you can use to learn about your prospects and customers, reach out to them, engage with them. And you have to keep your finger on the pulse of this. You have to keep tracking what's going on. And then lastly, I would say all of this is, I wouldn't say useless, but it's not applied in the best way possible if you don't learn how to manage the self. And there's a great Peter Drucker article about this in Harvard Business Review. But really, this is about the mental game. This is about having clarity of thought. It's about being aware of your own mental biases. It's about understanding environments where you perform at your best, where you're in flow, and environments where you don't. And understanding, you know, picking the right spots and figuring out if you can hack the environment. And also, not letting the ego getting in the way of doing the right thing for the team and the business. This is, obviously, it's a journey. There's no perfection here. I think it's a practice of learning to manage the self. A combination of these things, it served me well. I've seen it serve other people well as well. And so I think every marketer, every listener of your podcast should start thinking about what's their journey. What do they want to learn? And then map out how they would go about it.

[SPEAKER_05]
I love that. Yeah, you give us a lot. So if you are big picture, the things that it's helpful or that necessary to focus on in terms of what to educate yourself on to drive your career growth is you need to educate yourself on who it is that you're talking to in terms of your customers. You need to educate yourself on the emotional landscape

[None]
within that

[SPEAKER_05]
industry or within those folks that you're going to be talking to every day. What are they up against? And you mentioned what stories are they telling? So, so far, there's just, there is, there's a lot of listening involved in this education process that drives growth. And I noticed not a lot of really anything else, right? Not a lot that has to do with you until we get to this part where you need to learn about yourself. I think a lot of the time that's the part that gets left off. And I think of how salespeople in particular are onboarded and it's likely the same way with marketers, right? A lot of your training, yes, you're going to get trained on what the

[None]
personas are and

[SPEAKER_05]
you're going to get, you know, trained on what the problem is that your product attempts to solve. But there isn't necessarily training at the organizational level anyway, a lot of the time about, you know, the value of knowing yourself. So that's going to have to be something that you, you do on your own. And I think it's easy to forget about that or lose sight of that when you're, you know, putting a lot of your energy in on educating yourself on these, these other, you know, parts of the pieces of the puzzle. So I like the way that you, that you laid that out. So that's the sort of framework slash formula for things to educate yourself on when it comes to, when you're pursuing career growth. Talk about what that looks like when you apply it to, to a company, to the goal of company growth.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I think that's a great pivot. And by the way, you're so right on this, this idea of educating the self or the journey within. Schools don't necessarily talk about it. It's not a part of any formal education curriculum. But if you study philosophy, if you study religion, if you study any of that, you'll notice that all the greats have talked about this. They've said the journey within is what really leads you to drive change outside. So I couldn't agree with you more on the importance of doing that. And I wish there were more formalized options out there. But, you know, I think that's a, that's a separate topic. We can come back to

[None]
that at some point

[SPEAKER_00]
in the future. In terms of learning, driving growth, I hinted at some of this in my earlier question. But in general, most startups tend to be really product focused. And that's good. It's a good thing in many, many cases. But for marketers, you have to be really intentional and mindful in understanding prospect needs. And, you know, a good way to think about this is every company will tell you they're customer obsessed, that they're customer focused. But you really have to listen carefully to what they're saying. And then you have to look at how their actions, how all, how that thought is getting translated into actions. Many companies will think of their customers as essentially big dollar signs, as our CEO likes to say. And that's an incomplete picture. That's oftentimes a byproduct of you really understanding the problems that they're trying to solve and what they're trying to do better and then what they would like to learn. And most companies have a ton of intellectual property on these problems that can be solved. And I like to think of this as the discipline as opposed to just the product. It's the product plus the solution story. So if you can create a learning program where people can come in and learn how to do something new or solve problems that they have today, currently, it can be very powerful. have some examples of this. These happen to be our customers, but I think there's a ton of people doing good work on this. MapArt is a company, is an example that does big data education. So you can go in and learn all these tools. They're now a part of HPE, I think. And you can get trained on it. There's a company called Trade Desk that does training for ad tech, where you can go in and learn these new ad tech technologies. Smashfly is a company that does it for HR technology. Procore is a company that does it for construction technology. Snowflake, which is this white -hot unicorn, does it for how you do data warehousing in the cloud. Essentially, what you're doing is training a cohort of people on how they can solve problems and build their own careers. And if you do this right, obviously, you get leads because these people are coming in and registering on your website to get this training. But what you're also doing is creating these evangelists where they will take your product from company to company as they go on. And you end up creating this sort of setup to be the default option when people are trying to solve this problem. So it can be a very powerful investment to make. And a lot of times, it doesn't take a lot of investment on your side because you already have onboarding resources that you've developed. Your customer success team can probably come in and help you deliver a lot of this content. You can record it and provide it in an on -demand fashion. So this, we've seen this over and over again, can be a really powerful long -term investment that marketing can drive in partnership with customer success or product and therefore drive company growth with it.

[SPEAKER_02]
Hey, everybody. Logan with Sweetfish here. You probably already know that we think you should start a podcast if you haven't already. But what if you have and you're asking these kinds of questions? How much has our podcast impacted revenue this year? How's our sales team actually leveraging the podcast content? If you can't answer these questions, you're actually not alone. This is why Casted created the very first content marketing platform made specifically for B2B podcasting. Now you can more easily search and share your audio content while getting greater visibility into the impact of your podcast. The marketing teams at Drift, Terminus, and here at Sweetfish have started using Casted to get more value out of our podcasts, and you probably can too. You can check out the product in action at casted.us slash growth. That's C -A -S -T -E -D dot U -S slash growth. All right, let's get back to the show.

[SPEAKER_05]
For sure. For sure. I mean, just this idea of elevating the industry, making a contribution, building a community around what you do that, you know, involves your product but doesn't center on it. So it's how you answer the question. How is customer focus or customer experience or customer obsession, as you put it, how was that enacted, right?

[None]
I think exactly right.

[SPEAKER_05]
Right. You talked about people feel that way or that's part of their philosophy, but where is the action behind it? And that's where it is. It is in building that community like you talked about and, you know, making those resources available to folks, really accessible to folks who, whether you're a customer or not, but just, you know, proving not just that you know this industry, but that you're a member of it. You care about it. You're involved in pushing things forward for everyone. I love that. I love that. And it is. It starts with education. You've got to know these things in order to teach them. You've got to place a high, you've got to place a high premium and a high value on the education to begin with in order to justify making the kinds of investments in it that you're talking about. So, yeah, you're absolutely right. Thank you so much for laying that out for us. These little insights into how exactly does, you know, education drive growth when it comes to a career and how does it drive growth when it comes to a company? I think you gave us some

[None]
really good

[SPEAKER_05]
examples. And, you know, before I get to this next segment, I want to ask you, is there

[None]
anything

[SPEAKER_05]
else that, you know, with respect to education driving growth, whether it's career or company that you want to leave our listeners with before we move on?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I would say you encapsulated that beautifully. The prospect's customers tend to buy your why a lot sooner than before they buy the what and the how. That comes later. And if you start with this philosophy of giving and of making people successful, you'd be surprised at how much faster deals progress and how much people buy into sort of what you're doing if you start from a place of giving. So I think that's a good place to be.

[SPEAKER_05]
I love it. I love it. So, Ashish, now that I have successfully picked your brain and seeing what I could get out of it, it is time for you to tell us a little bit about what you're putting in it. So let us know about, you know, a learning resource or something that you're engaging with that's just, you know, informing your approach or got you excited these days.

[None]
Yes,

[SPEAKER_00]
I have a book recommendation. I love reading and I'm an engineer. So I'm always looking for books that go beyond just the logical because I've gotten trained on the logical for a bit. Sure. And there's a book called Alchemy that's by a gent by the name of Rory Sutherland. He runs Ogilvy Mathers, which is this massive global ad agency. based in the UK, but the book is called Alchemy. And he walks you through the different approaches to sort of non -logical marketing, I will call it. And just one snippet from it that stuck with me for the last couple of weeks is a lot of times the opposite of a good idea is not a bad idea, but another good idea. And it's this sort of parallel thinking approach that a lot of us struggle with. Engineers in particular can often be pretty dualistic. It's either good or bad.

[None]
And reading

[SPEAKER_00]
this book has opened up some new creative things for me to try. Rory's an ad legend. So he walks you through the development of campaigns. He talks about how seemingly non -logical choices can have a massive impact. He talks about ad testing. I think your listeners would enjoy reading the book and walk away with some fresh insights from it.

[None]
I

[SPEAKER_05]
love it. I want to read this book. Thank you. A lot of the times folks will name books that either I have read or that are currently sitting in my audible library. But this is one I hadn't heard of yet. So thank you. Thank you for that. Listen, Ashish, I know that just like me, everybody listening has become a fast fan of yours. And they are going to want to know how to keep up with you. So tell us. Tell us how folks can connect with you.

[SPEAKER_00]
Absolutely. I'm on LinkedIn. You can find me there. I'm also on Twitter at just my last name. So it's at Damdere. Damdere, look me up there. Let me know if you have a book recommendation. I'm always curious to know if there's a book I should read or a podcast that you enjoy. I'd love connecting with you.

[SPEAKER_05]
Thanks so much. We'll have to have you on again. There were a couple of questions that came up that we both, I think, wanted to dig into. But as you said, that's a whole other episode.

[None]
So until then,

[SPEAKER_05]
thanks so much, Ashish.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thank you, Nikki. Thanks again for having me.

[SPEAKER_02]
We totally get it. We publish a ton of content on this podcast, and it can be a lot to keep up with. That's why we've started the B2B Growth Big Three, a no -fluff email that boils down our three biggest takeaways from an entire week of episodes. Sign up today at sweetfishmedia.com slash big three. That's sweetfishmedia.com slash big three.

[SPEAKER_00]
This is my second time in Slovenia and the last time I was here was 11 years ago and since then I've been telling everyone Slovenia is such an amazing country, everyone must come visit. I was really charmed by the place 11 years ago so when Urban asked me to come I said of course I would love to. So I'm to be talking a little bit about fintech and you'll understand why fintech is important to me. So topics, I'm going talk about who I am, what is fintech, some trends in fintech and what to expect in the coming years. So let me tell you about myself. So I personally have been an entrepreneur on the fintech side a couple of times, two exits, one was a payments company called Fee Fighters, it was acquired by Groupon in 2012, and then an auction company called Innovative Auctions, Applicant Auction, sold in 2015. And then sort of since that first exit in 2012, I've been investing in companies, primarily fintech companies, although early on I was not so focused. So since 2012 I've been investing and then since 2015 I've been investing with 500 Startups. 500 Startups is the world's most active seed investor. We invest globally, we've invested in over 2,000 portfolio companies and we have about $600 million in AUM. And we're active in over 50 countries, or we've invested in over 50 countries. So we're really active, we do a lot of stuff, we actually have a couple of investments in Slovenia as well. And in fintech, again we're the most active overall, so we happen to be the most active in fintech as well. And, you know, by being the most active you tend to see the most things, and also because we're at the earliest stages, we tend to see trends before others just because people come to us first. So first, what is fintech? I think about fintech as it being a term that can describe any technology solutions that make financial services more efficient. And those can be as a disruptor, meaning directly going after consumers or small businesses, or it can be as an enabler. A lot of companies are just helping financial institutions execute better, and we invest across all of them. So here are some of our investments. We've invested in lending, blockchain, crowdfunding, wealth management, financial management, insurance, and payments. And you can see some of our most successful companies that you might be familiar with are Stripe and Credit Karma, but there are a lot of others, and we've been investing a lot in the last few years. So I think hopefully over the coming years, you'll see a lot of names that you recognize here in your life. So what's going on with fintech? Fintech has been on an absolute tear. So if you look over the past several years, fintech investment went up to $40 billion last year. Five years ago, it only $8 billion. So massive increase. And in that increase, it's really been... There's an interesting story here, because from 2014 to 2018, the US only doubled. So the US went from about $6 billion to $12 billion. So where did all that growth come from? Well, it really came from Asia. Asia has been growing at 265 % year over year. And the whole world is growing. Unfortunately, Europe is not growing as fast as the rest of the world. But in the US, this has been a really big change. And one of the things that's been changing is, we used to always think that innovation started in the US and went elsewhere in the world. Now, myself and many other venture investors are actually going to China and looking at... Just spending time in China, seeing everyday people, because the kind of innovation that's coming out of China is very different than the kind that's coming out of the US or the rest of the world. So we've really got our eye to China, and that's where a lot of this growth is happening. And it's happening in everything. So this is a website of Wells Fargo Bank, one of the largest banks in the US. And this sort of shows all the places that fintechs are going after the bank. And you see that it's like, there's not just one fintech that's replacing the bank, it's a bunch of different companies going after various verticals of the bank. And you see, we've had a lot of success. Again, to the previous slide we were talking about China. We've got about 65 % of the unicorns based in the US, but that's also because it takes time to grow a unicorn. And as funding was big in the US years ago, it was not big elsewhere, I think over time you'll see the shift, and there'll be a lot more exciting companies coming out of Asia. Fortunately, we've invested in two of these unicorns, I wish we'd invested in more, but we've got two, Stripe and Credit Karma, that are part of our group. So how did we get here? This shows just a Google Trends search I did yesterday on fintech, the term fintech. And if you look, in 2014, where my other chart started, in 2014, not that many people were talking about fintech. If today we're at 100, in 2019, in July of 2014, we were at 6. So things have really changed very rapidly where fintech is now a term that everyone knows, not just those in the tech world. So what changed? How did we get here? I think it starts if you look backwards. So starting in 2008, we had obviously a global financial crisis, and the banks lost a lot of trust. People like me saw this as an opportunity to create something better. The tarnished brand of banks plus new regulation was a golden opportunity, and a lot of the folks that grew up in this time, just became adults in 2008, saw the banks as something they didn't like. There was a big backlash against the banks. And so as these guys grew up being digitally native, you know, over time there became an opportunity for fintechs. And while the banks were hated, they're still massive. So globally, financial services represents 17 % of global GDP. That's $13 trillion. So of course we all want a piece of this pie. And you would think with this massive opportunity, technology would come in and solve this like it has in many other industries. But actually, even in a developed economy like the US, less than 1 % of loans are currently generated online. So there's a massive, massive opportunity still to come to bring fintech, financial services online. And that's really exciting. And we see that it's not only exciting to disrupt traditional financial institutions, you can actually create massive businesses just serving them. And so the banks actually spend about 30 % of their expenses on operations and compliance. Massive amount. So they spend $480 billion a year, it's just US banks, on operations and compliance. So we've actually made a few investments in that space that helps them do a better job of compliance. And then the thing that excites me the most is spreading this globally. So my career, my fintech career actually started in the nonprofit sector. I did microfinance in India. So many times, you know, I'd be working on a farm and a customer, you know, we had borrowers around the area. So to service one borrower, I would take a bus and then ride on the back of somebody's motorcycle to serve one borrower, to lend them $200. And then every month, we'd have to go back and get the money back. Now that's all available in your hand, in a smartphone. And there are lots of companies going after this exact segment that I tried to serve 12 years ago manually, but doing it via the smartphone in a much more efficient way. And that efficiency also translates to lower costs for the customers. So this really excites me is that in the next three years, will be two billion more smartphone users. And that's largely coming in Asia and Africa. And that's very exciting, the opportunity to bring all these people into the formal financial system. And so this fintech has the opportunity to transform a lot of people's lives. And we've seen that technology has already done that. So if you look at the largest companies, even in my recent lifetime, like when I was in college, the largest public companies were in the oil sector, in the banking sector, in General Electric, the conglomerate, all the other things that they did, now if you look at it, the largest companies in the world by market cap are all technology companies. And that's a huge opportunity. Because these companies are actually all becoming fintech companies too. If you look at Google, they're a payments company. If you look at Apple, they've got payments and insurance. Facebook has launched payments, and Amazon has launched payments and lending. Now, these guys actually, their core business is not financial services, but they don't want to allow financial services to slow their growth. Amazon is in lending and payments, but only because it increases your basket size, or actually increases their merchants on Amazon. Now, Uber is a big opportunity. Uber got into the leasing business, they're leasing cars, just to see if they could attract and retain drivers. They're also, in the US, the largest driver of new bank accounts. And why is that? It's because when drivers sign up to drive for Uber, they need to have a bank account so they can get the money. And many of these drivers actually don't have a bank account, so Uber is signing up bank accounts for them. I think that's a huge opportunity. We're seeing new entrants in fintech around the world. So, we're seeing retailers. How many of guys know about Ant Financial? Very few. Very Okay, it's a Chinese company. They're a consumer and small business payments lending company. They started, just in the past several years, grew to $150 billion valuation. Massive company. And they spun out of Alibaba. And so, they use data from Alibaba on their 9 billion small business customers, and then they've spun out this business that is a financial services business. So, these existing businesses are spinning out financial services, financial technology businesses, and I think that's allowed them to build massive businesses just off of what they were doing already. If you look at it, it's also happening to the telcos. So, the telcos have a lot of what you need to become a lender, for example. So, for a lender, there are three things that you really need. You need distribution. You need underwriting and collections. Now, if you're a telco, you have massive distribution. People have you in their pocket, basically. And then you need underwriting. So, what do these telcos do? They can underwrite based off of your existing payments. Like, have you paid your monthly payment on time? And then they can also do all sorts of things based on who you call, all sorts of creepy stuff that a lot of these companies actually do. Is take the data from your mobile phone and use that to make an assessment of your credit score. So, Orange has 270 million customers globally, and in Africa, they already had 34 million mobile money subscribers. Last year, they acquired a French banking license, and they're getting a Spanish biking license this year. So, these guys are increasingly in the fintech world. And then we have the traditional financial institutions. So, in the US, Goldman Sachs did not have a retail presence until a few years ago. And actually, after the financial crisis, they were regulatorily required to create a retail presence. So, they launched in 2016 a new bank called Marcus. And they launched it with no fee consumer lending. And within a couple of years, they had over $2 billion in loans. Outstanding. And they just launched home improvement loans. And these guys are actually a force to be reckoned with. And when we talk about fintechs, actually, I think what Goldman Sachs has built is a fintech company. And it's really impressive. So, these are all challenges that we see with fintechs. Like, they're under pressure from all these different spaces. Retailers, telcos, banks. And if you look at Goldman, look at their open jobs today. If you look at this right side, the dark blue, all of those are engineering job hires. So, like, almost half of the people that Goldman Sachs is hiring today are engineers. And that speaks to what they're trying to build in financial technology. And the banks are worried. I think, you know, Jamie Dimon said it. Silicon Valley is coming. There are a bunch of startups with brains working on alternatives that are trying to take over our business. Now, we said that in 2015. I think what we've learned over the past several years is the fintechs have to... Many of them are trying to disrupt the traditional banks, but none of them have done it yet. It's all sort of verticals, going after verticals of the traditional banks. But if you look at how traditional banks make money, in the US, roughly speaking, it costs $500 to acquire a customer for a bank. And they make about $250 per sliver that you go into. So, if you're a lender, they make $250 lifetime. If you're a saver, they make $250 lifetime. So, really, how they make money is if you do multiple tasks with the bank. So, they need to cross -sell you into a mortgage, into a credit card, into your deposits, etc. Now, if these fintechs are going after small slices, they're actually going after the things that really matter to the banks. Because the banks aren't profitable unless they sell you multiple things. So, Silicon Valley is coming. But, it turns out that it's actually... All of these fintech companies need to partner with the banks. So, all the companies in my portfolio have some sort of partnership with a bank. And the banks are the underlying technology. Now, what that might mean is the banks are basically become the plumbing. And all this technology and consumer stuff is built on top of that. I think that's still a massive opportunity. So, fintechs were the disruptors. Now, they're the partners to the banks. But what are trends that we see in the future? So, one thing is fintech has come a really long way over the past several years. A lot of these companies you probably know very well. N26, TransferWise, PayPal, Credit Karma, etc. They need to expand sort of like what I said with the traditional banks. The fintechs also need to expand beyond their first business into another business. We can talk about Credit Karma because it's in our portfolio, one that we know well. So, Credit Karma started out as a free credit scoring tool in the US. So, all it means is in the US it's very important to have a good credit score. means it's how you get an apartment, it's how you get a credit card, etc. And before Credit Karma came along, you had to pay money to get access to your own data. Credit Karma said, we'll give it to you for free and we'll make money because by knowing your credit score, we'll give you the perfectly targeted lending product whether it's a credit card or insurance or lending. And so that was great. Credit Karma has had phenomenal success. 80 million people in the US are using Credit Karma to check their credit scores regularly. But at some point, we had to move out of being a one trick pony using a credit card to get just credit information and sell you credit cards. So, what did they do? They've acquired a few companies. They acquired a company in the mortgage space, they acquired a company in the tax preparation space. So, what we said was, we're going to do, and they expanded into Canada. So, what we said was, we're not just going to be the one thing, free credit score, we're actually going to be free many things. So, we added free tax preparation. And the free tax preparation actually gives us so much more data into you that we can serve you even more targeted financial services requests. And that has made our recommendations so much better that the conversions have gone up and it actually makes the company a lot more money. And so, you can do this via acquiring or you can do this via partnerships. But it is important that you move from one product into multiple products. So, can talk about Revolut. They started out as a digital wallet, basically as a prepaid card. And then they've moved into crypto, they've moved into bank accounts, they've moved into brokerage. So, the one trick pony was originally starting out as a credit account that you could use for cross -border payments. And now, they've moved into all these other verticals. And the same is true in all the major fintech companies.

many of these companies that started out to disrupt the banks are actually now becoming the banks. So, a lot of companies are applying for their own bank charter. And that's an interesting place because banks have historically traded at similar multiples. But these guys will go for potentially a much higher multiple. And it will be interesting to see how it plays out. And some governments are very favorable to it. Some are not. The US is actually not very favorable. So, in the US, I think that there's an opportunity for a new type of bank. And I call it BWS. You guys are probably familiar with AWS, Amazon Web Services. So, I made this term BWS, Banking Web Services. I think that there needs to exist a company behind all these other companies that basically all they do is have a bank charter and have an API that you can build on top of that bank charter. So, if I think about the future, I think about four different types of banks. One is legacy banks. The banks that are big all over the world. Those there's nothing you need to know about. BWS is Banking Web Services. These guys just are a bank charter and an API built on top of it that everyone else can build on top of. And so, who uses that? They're non -bank players. We already talked about Uber. So, Uber is probably not going to get a bank charter. But Uber has the need to bring all these people into the banking system. So, right now, when you sign up to get an Uber, to be a driver for Uber, they send you offline to a third party to get a bank account. What if that could all happen within the app? If there was something like a BWS, they could all do that within the app. The same is true for Airbnb, et cetera. And then I think there should be niche banks. In the US, there are 6,000 banks. And about 4,500 of them are making a lot less money than they used to. Like the large banks make sense because they can do everything to everyone. But smaller banks actually make no sense because you're trying to build the same suite of products for everyone, but for a much smaller niche set. So, what I think they should become is a niche bank. So, there could be banks for agriculture, banks for landlords, banks for just gig economy workers. And I think that there's a big future there. The final trend I'll say is regulation is really coming fast. So, regulators are upping oversight on bad actors and issuing massive fines. [SPEAKER_00]
Okay, can everyone hear me? It sounds like you can. My name is Christine Laredo, and I lead FinTech Evangelism for Yodley, and I also founded our award -winning incubator. Thank you for having me. I actually reside out in San Francisco in Silicon Valley, and I'm going to give a talk on what we've seen, or what I've seen with entrepreneurs and FinTech founders that has led them to success. But before I do that, little bit about my company and about myself. How many of you in the room know Yodley and what we do in FinTech? Okay, a few hands. So I'm going to give you a little bit of info so everything I speak about is more relevant. So Yodley is one of the FinTech pioneers. We started our business in 1999. We operate in 15 markets, have a growing and flourishing business here in the UK. But essentially we have helped banks, FIs, and now FinTechs with financial data. We actually pull in the financial data for the banks. We secure it. We cleanse it. We make it readily available so FinTechs and FIs and others can build really meaningful solutions to help us live better financial lives. And basically seven years ago I was brought on to really develop the non -bank business, the FinTech business. And about five years ago I said, wow, we really need to help these startups. We have an ecosystem. We have great data. Let's start an incubator. And we started an incubator about five years ago. We've now graduated 40 companies. We're looking to do more with the incubator. These companies have been around the world. And so I do a lot of work with FinTech startups. Before joining Yodley I actually worked in mobile consumer services, companies called Yahoo and AOL you may have heard of. And then I was like, I'm in Silicon Valley. I want to get into the startup world. So I went to very early stage startups. I raised a first round. It was very hard. I tried to build product market fit. I tried to build teams. I got caught in a mobile payments company that one day we had this great old business that was funding our new growth business. And then all of a sudden the political environment changed on the hill in the U.S. And our bread and butter business was shut down, which caused so much turmoil because we had to go raise money to grow our new business. Crazy stuff. Crazy So I ended up joining Yodley after that and then the rest is history. But in addition to overseeing our incubator, my job is to really to talk to startups around the world and listen to their needs and ensure that our product roadmap has solutions that will help them build services faster. One of the things we recently uncovered through that work was a renewed commitment to developers. And so I'm really excited about our product roadmap and how it will enhance the developer experience and more. But for now I'm going to move on and talk about what it takes to be successful. But first, before I get into those fintech needs, there are actually some key attributes of founders. And I've gained these insights by not only working with the mentors and investors in our ecosystem but talking to founders. And I think it's important to share because this is critical across tech and carries through the additional needs. So the first is solve a problem that's meaningful, not just an idea, a problem that customers will reach in their wallet and give you money for. And it has to be some sense of urgency. I see a lot of entrepreneurs out there with a great whiz -bang idea but then there's no solving of a problem. Nobody wants to pay for it. There's no sense of urgency. And the proverbial solution in search of a problem does exist. So it's very important to make sure that you have a problem that your customers will reach out and spend their budgets or their hard -earned dollars on. And the next piece is building those effective teams, right? So having the leadership to guide the vision, having the people on board to support. But in fintech, it isn't exactly an area where there are turnkey tools and free scripts that one can use to come up with an app or service. It isn't like some other tech venture where barriers aren't low. There's financial needs, technological needs, and business expertise needs. So you've got to have that right team. And you can tell within two handfuls of hours of working with companies in boot camps who has the team and who doesn't to go and take that problem you're solving to success. Third item is flexibility. So having to be flexible, especially in the beginning when you're trying to make sure you have that problem that people will reach in their wallets and pay for. So tinkering, testing, refining. The entrepreneur has to be committed to being flexible and guiding the team to be flexible and kind of ruling out what doesn't work and finding what does work and staying committed. And, you know, the other thing is it's not just about that problem you're solving. But in technology, the market changes every six to seven years as a whole new generation grows up and starts to spend money. So this means that change is inevitable and navigating that change is critical for success. The final attribute has to do with grit or focus, never giving up perseverance. So this contradicts a little bit of what I said before, saying, okay, tinker, test and refine. But then once you find that product market fit, these entrepreneurs, if they're going to succeed, they have to stay committed. They have to persevere. They have to keep those blinders on so that their developers or their product team isn't chasing squirrel or the next best idea. And it's really key, especially when you found that sense of urgency and you have customers that will pay for it through their wallet or through their budgets. So given that these four key attributes are there, startup fintech needs are pretty robust. This is a wheel that I created for our incubator companies so that they can understand what the needs are. And if you don't have the needs, then it's very important to get access to them. As you know, money and health are probably the two most critical pieces in one's life. And they're the most regulated. The financial vertical is one of the last to benefit from new tech and is the victim of tougher regulatory environment. I know you guys were spending a lot of time in this debate before, and so I don't have to mention how serious that is. But we also have, like, some marketplaces evolving. We are entering a robust two -sided economy, also known as the sharing economy, where we have heavy hitters like Airbnb, Lyft, Uber, that are just incorporating financial services to enable different types of transactions for both businesses that they're building. So it's super exciting. There's so many ideas out there, so many ways to innovate, as fintech is everywhere and sparking tons of innovation. But it's so important to understand these needs. So I'm just going to mention a few of them that I've seen these startups need and lack and really kind of show how they can gain this expertise through an ecosystem. The first one is regulatory and compliance. I'm not going to spend a lot of time on it. I just want to highlight how important it is. It's also important to think globally and act locally because environments change constantly. I was a victim of it in a previous company, as I mentioned. Every market's different. Political landscapes change it. There's so much compliance required and often includes accountants and lawyers. So it's important to have the understandings here. Understanding here. World -class data access. To build great products, fintech startups need access to data, whether it be APIs or feeds delivering financial data, market exchange data, investment data, market intelligence data from media, consensus data or credit data. I think you get the idea. It is pretty much guaranteed that this data will be critical to the success of the new solution. There are many providers out there. after dealing with startups again and again, I tell them the best way is to work with the entity that has the most robust data. I've heard so many of them getting burned because they didn't have what they needed at the end of the day as they're growing their business. And then you also need a provider that makes sure that data is meaningful and enriched and puts it to good use. There's a lot of companies out there providing data. So it's important to ask those questions and ensure you have the most comprehensive data. I know my company works very hard to ensure that we have the massive scale and that we have this data in a secure environment to be used. So definitely tell startups to ask the question. The next piece, which comes naturally, is security and scalability. A big need. When it comes to finances, consumers need to know and customers, whether you're SMB or a consumer, need to know that their money is safe and secure hands. Financial institutions have a history of earning that trust through long -term relationships. So if you're a new bank and if you're handling data of any sort, then you need partners and vendors with a high caliber of regular security audits. You know, working with a partner that handles this data in an insure way can allow you to ride along with it. I know that our platform at Yodley allows our customers to benefit from the full breadth of rigor and our risk management program. So some benefits of working with a bigger player is the same platform exists for the top of the market FI as does the two guys or gals in a garage. So that's a big benefit. So make sure if you're a startup to ask those questions. Okay, development help and UI needs. And really, this is product, product, product. I tell every company in FinTech, you have to be highly customer centric. You have to talk to your customers and look at data that shows how they're using your product and how they're not using it. And those pieces are very important because what they say isn't always what they do. And we've had a lot of entrepreneurs that are coming into our incubator program and they're spending time with partners and distribution channels. And we say, stop, please focus on your product. It is so important in FinTech. It has to be right, especially in the beginning. I mean, the best use of time is to be highly product focused. So if you just think about it, it's much more important in FinTech. So it's social app. I work in consumer mobile technology before and not that instant messaging wasn't important back then. But if you think about it, you know, if you have a data feed that's incorrect and social, it's not as big of a deal as a data feed for a budget of an SMB customer. If your budget is wrong, your customer can't manage their business. So get your product right. Spend the time there. It's also important for the startup to have access to development help as they scale. They may get into complex FinTech areas. And it pays to find developers or work with partners who have been in these circumstances or handled data this nature before and can help achieve these complex areas. So minimal viable product feedback. This is really critical, especially in FinTech. I tell startups that, okay, so you think you have everything right. There's so much importance of using industry leaders to help validate in the early stage. The tight community is very connected and influential and getting feedback and help with market validation is critical to better funding as well. Essentially, you have those folks within your marketplace that can help you. And then you put together the right process to launch your product. And then you can always go back and forth to your industry leaders. So what does that mean? So we tell startups, and this is really through going through 40 companies and working with companies in our portfolio, that you really have to follow a pretty four -step process, which includes designing a beta program that can effectively capture, process, and share data -driven feedback from your business and customers. And once you have that beta program, then you go and you create your pricing strategy, then you launch it back in the market, you get your user feedback, and then you have to apply your engagement pieces. So if you heard me talk before about being customer -centric and really making sure you look at not just what your customers are saying, but how they're using it, and you apply all this, at the same time getting your feedback from your market leaders, then you will definitely have a market, excuse me, a minimal viable product. And so setting those stages up, your industry feedback, your beta, your pricing, your user feedback, and your engagement analysis will set up the startups for success. Okay. Moving along. So funding and capital, it's kind of an obvious one, but the way I'm going to speak about it isn't obvious. It's more about access and getting relationships built at an early stage with those that hold the keys to wallets. And, you if you look at the recent stats from CB Insights, think we, 2018, there was $40 billion invested globally in fintech. So you might think, ah, must be pretty easy. We grew 120 % from the year before. But if you break it down, many of those were very big deals. I think we had a $14 billion deal loan from one of Alibaba's ventures. And so it actually isn't as easy as it seems. And, you know, giving these startups access to the VCs early on helps them build relationships, helps them understand a little bit more about their vision. And you can actually use these investors to help shape the vision and shape the product, which will help create a better synergy because it's not just the first raise, it's several thereafter, because you need a lot of money to build a great fintech. It's not as easy as a consumer mobile service. And so all my successful companies suggest working with them early on and letting those investors shape the story and build relationships. Business acceleration. So, you know, if I think about all those pieces of the wheel, business acceleration is super important because fintech is complicated. There's so many accelerators out there. Of course, we operate our own. There's no equity involved in our accelerator. We take companies globally. It's not a residence program. It's pretty easy to participate. Of course, you have to get in. But I really think it's important. So I tell startups, find a way to get some kind of business acceleration. Work with a vendor or a partner that's big that has an ecosystem so they can help them with relationships. Go to an incubator or an accelerator or two. Spend time networking. You know, certain regions of the world have meetups and events. But I think it's a very big piece. And meeting other folks that have solved problems that you're stuck on can really help growth and the ability to become successful. So hopefully that was interesting. I just shared a little bit about what we think startups need. It's quite a lot. I can't stress the importance of an ecosystem, whether it be through an accelerator or a vendor or partner or through some other method to achieve help and access to these needs. But thanks for letting me share some views from Silicon Valley. I think I have four minutes left for questions. And we'll take those now.

[None]
Sure.

[SPEAKER_02]
Let's take some questions. Is there anything on Slido? Otherwise, we'll take some questions from the floor. There's one here. There's one on Slido as well. Oh, okay.

[None]
Go ahead.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thank you very much. So I too have lived in Silicon Valley, lived in London, lived in New York. And obviously you talked about kind of going all over the globe, talking to fintech startups. So what I'd be really curious to know is your take on the sort of idiosyncrasies of the different markets and what it is maybe that you feel is special about London and maybe what help startups in London need that might be a bit different from, let's say, the Valley or other places in the globe.

[None]
Yeah,

[SPEAKER_00]
it's a good question. think just my little bit of knowledge of London, I would akin it to New York where it's a financial market first and foremost and then the tech was kind of built around it. So I think you have a lot of that financial expertise. I look at Silicon Valley and you've got the tech, but then we lack in the financial piece and it's a struggle. But I think in London that benefit is folks that have been in finance and working with banks and markets. So there's a lot of resources. But I think when you bring on those people that have the financial service expertise, you have to realize they may not have the tech. But I think another benefit to London is it's a techier market than some of the other European markets. So I think there's a lot of great ideas, a lot of innovation going on. It's partly because of those two pieces.

[None]
Great.

[SPEAKER_02]
What about this one? What are some of the most exciting business ideas and startups that have come through your program?

[SPEAKER_00]
Oh, that's a great one. Well, there's some really interesting things. don't know if you guys have heard of PropTech, property technology. There's a ton going on there, especially, I think London is similar to San Francisco where a lot of people can't buy a house because it's so crazy expensive. So one of the most interesting ideas is a company that's helping in high real estate markets, but then there's another one that came on last year that's helping in non -high So serving the folks that make a lot of money that can't afford a house because you're living in San Francisco or London. And then there's a company, Hurry Home, that's actually helping people who are underserved who actually live in the outside of Detroit and they can't buy a home because of what's happened to Detroit. And they just, you know, they're blue collar and they just don't have the money. So what both of these companies do is they buy part of the house with you so that you're an equity owner, not like a bank, but like a real entity. And they enable people to have a house to serve their, you know, five person family that has a decent living experience both in a kind of an underserved market and San Francisco or London. So I like the two sides. The other thing that we had in our incubator was a company that's a next generation mobile voting platform called Votes. And they used us as one of the three factors of authentication. So if you're voting in municipality or proxy voting or one of the other use cases, they would have three factors, blockchain, biometrics, and then account verification. I thought that was pretty cool. So some good examples.

[SPEAKER_02]
Great. Thanks very much. Maybe take the last one and give us your thoughts on the funding gap between male and females.

[SPEAKER_00]
Oh, wow. That is such a big question. I mean, I think I spoke about this recently in Austin, Texas, which by the way, there's more female entrepreneurs in Austin, Texas getting funding than any other place in the U.S. I was born in Fort Worth, Texas. So that's pretty exciting. But that's also a big gap. And I think part of the problem, and we run this incubator, and we don't have that many applicants coming from female founders. It is a requirement for us to have one company with a female founder, and it is tough to find. So I think that it's hard to fund companies when there aren't companies to fund. So I know in talking to VCs around the U.S. and New York and some other places, I know there's a big effort to change that. But I mean, my biggest point is female founders get up and get out there because the stats are overwhelmingly strong. Women founders do a great job. The numbers are high. They're outperforming companies led by men, and that's just, you know, they've got to get up and get out there.

[SPEAKER_02]
Fantastic. What a great way to finish the panel. Thank you.

[None]
Thank you. Thank you.

Quora? How did Mark Cuban turn the Mavs around from a business perspective? Well, I'm going to be brutally honest. I really didn't care about the business of the Dallas Mavericks when I bought them. I really cared about winning championships and winning games. And so I spent a whole lot more time on the basketball side of things. And the Mavs lost money almost every year until the past three years. When I got to the NBA, when I bought the Dallas Mavericks, everybody thought we sold basketball. Very few people go to basketball games to watch basketball. Think about the last sporting event you went to. Do you remember a jump shot? Do you remember a dunk? Do you even remember the score? Maybe you remember who we played, but you remember who you were with. It's an experience. You remember how you felt. When that ball's in the air and it's a tie game, if it goes through the hoop, you win. And if it doesn't, you lose. Everybody, collectively, 20,000 people are holding their breath. And when it goes through the hoop, you're high -fiving and hugging and squeezing so tight people you've never seen before in your life. You're walking out of the arena screaming and yelling. And if you lose, you do the exact opposite. Apple, one of the biggest companies in the world, they could have their best quarter, their best year ever. No one's throwing a parade in Cupertino. The Dallas Mavericks win a championship. Dallas is on fire. Everybody's having an amazing time. The whole city feels the energy. You feel that energy when you walk into the arena. That's what I convinced the NBA that we sell. And that literally changed how sports were sold.
