It's definitely more art than science. it's hard to, I would say market and team are by far the two biggest things, but it depends on the company. It depends on the market. It depends on the team, which one is more important than any given, at any given deal. Some people seem to tend to draw a hard line of like, if the market's big enough or it's growing fast enough or whatever, it doesn't matter who the team is and vice versa. I don't know. I tend not to draw hard lines on anything. It's just kind of depends

[None]

[SPEAKER_00]
But generally speaking, like we invest, like I was saying before, in anything that is anywhere near the financial services world. Payments, banking, lending, insurance, real estate, consumer, B2B, you name it. We've dabbled in crypto in the past, though it's not like kind of a core focus of this fund, but it's only a matter of time. I imagine before we, before we make some crypto investments. And so it's a little bit of everything. And we've also invested in a handful of companies that aren't technically fintech companies. But given some of the trends that I was talking about before with like embedded fintech and kind of companies starting to leverage technology to distribute financial products, even if they're not financial services companies at their core, we've also invested in a handful of companies that are more like marketplaces or vertical SaaS companies that we think will look more like fintech companies in the future, but aren't today. So it's a little bit of everything. And we're pre -seed and seed. We're typically writing up to one and a half million dollar checks. We're typically looking for at least 10 % ownership. And then the reason for that is like I was saying before, we are operators and entrepreneurs first. When we partner up with a company, we like to get involved and help them build. Like we only invest in companies where we would want to be part of the founding team. And we, I mean, to the extent that we can, I mean, we're, we're VCs, we're not founders, or we're not, we're not operators in that sense. Like we try to be instrumental in those early days of helping shorten learning curves and accelerate companies out of the gates, but really rolling up our sleeves and bringing all of our resources to bear to make it happen. And so one of the things we've learned over the years is when you're writing 25 to 150 K checks into companies and you own a tiny piece of the company in exchange for that, it doesn't justify all the, all the time and effort that you're putting in to help those companies grow. And so we've had to, had to kind of be adamant about investing in less companies, but owning more of those companies and being more of a financial partner, but also being able to to, to be like a real operating partner as well.

All right, so we're going to talk about strategic pivots, something that's pretty close to my heart because a lot of my portfolio companies have been through them, and even myself, I've been through it myself as a founder. So I thought maybe we could start by talking through some companies that you guys all know, and I might tell you what the company started out as, and you have to tell me what the company is now. So first one's pretty easy. It's Bourbon, a very famous company today. It started out as a location sharing app, B -U -R -B -N. Does anybody know what that company is today? Correct. It's Instagram. So Instagram became a photo sharing app, but actually it was a location sharing app that they allowed folks to add photos to, and they realized the photo part was more popular than the location sharing part, and they pivoted the business to this filters app called Instagram. All right, another one. This one's kind of tough, actually. It's Chiquita, and this is a education app that allows teachers to share short -form video content on education. It's the app now known as TikTok. It actually started out as an education app, and so what happened was the founders built this product. They were educators. They started the product for teachers to teach their students various things in short form, and what happened was it accidentally caught on amongst people using it to do karaoke, and the founders realized that the app was getting a lot of popularity Thursday nights when there was this popular TV show called Carpool Karaoke, and they saw the videos, and it was all karaoke, and they pivoted the app to what was Musical.ly, which then got bought by Duyen in China and became TikTok. So another pivot. Okay, so another one. Odeo podcasting platform. came out a long time ago. Anyone know? Twitter, that's right. The founders all thought podcasting was the next new thing, and they launched a podcasting platform, but internally, they built this micro -blogging platform to talk amongst themselves. What happened with the podcasting platform was Apple released their own podcasting platform. Odeo was basically DOA, and they thought, okay, let's create this micro -blogging platform, Twitter. What is TinySpec? It was a gaming company started by Stuart Butterfield. Does anybody know now? Slack. They had built an internal tool. They built Slack internally for themselves, at the gaming company. Gaming company wasn't doing so hot. Some of their friends wanted the tool that they had built internally because they were all hyped about it. They started selling it externally, and then ultimately became, obviously, a massive company. And then the last one is one closer to my heart in the fintech space. It was a company called Wallet, and it was a consumer business that helped do you manage your finances. Anybody know this one? Wallet, the consumer company, didn't really take off that well and ultimately became Plaid. So they decided, we're going to sell the same product to other companies, building companies like Wallet. So anyway, just wanted to throw that out there that pivoting is not strange. Pivoting is not weird. You should not feel ashamed if your initial product doesn't work out. Many of the products that we use today were originally something else entirely. And so it's totally fine to pivot. And in fact, I think pivoting is really a sign of strength. So the way to think about it is, along the way, you're building a product, you have some idea of what it is you want to build, some idea of the future vision that you want to see in the world. And then along the way, maybe you realize customers aren't aligning with that vision. At some point, so then there's a question, how do you decide and when do you know that customers aren't aligning with that vision? Are you guys familiar with Rahul Vora, the CEO of Superhuman? He wrote this article in the first round review about how to find product market fit. How many of you guys read that article? Okay, we have a couple of people in back. So I highly recommend reading that article. It's a great tool for finding product market fit. And the question is simple. It's ask your customers how they would feel if they could no longer use the product. And if the response is not like overwhelmingly negative, and if it's not, oh, if this product didn't exist, my life would become a lot tougher, then you know you don't yet have product market fit. And a lot of times people think that they have product market fit because they're giving something away for free. So that's another thing I might challenge you with is thinking about pricing. In my portfolio, I have a company called Albert. It started out as a personal finance manager, actually like Wallet, the original product that Plaid was. So this company, you know, they were giving away a free product, help you manage your finances. And they actually didn't really have much monetization figured out. All the metrics look great. Like everybody was used. They had a lot of people signing up to try the product. But they realized, like, is this really critical? Like, do people really, really want this product? And the way that they decided to test that was actually charging their customers. And this is actually they did this when they were almost running out of money. So they were at the point where they were going to shut the company down. And they instead said, asked when customers logged into the app, they said, would you be willing to pay us for this service? And they had a slider. And the customers actually had to pay for the service. So you could pay zero, or you could pay up to $14 a month. And, you know, the company was dying at this point. So it was like a last ditch effort. Let's see if our companies are willing to if our customers are willing to pay.

[None]
And

the customers actually overwhelmingly were willing to pay, like 80 % of their customers were willing to pay an average of $4. And so they realized, okay, customers actually do want this product. And oh, by the way, that revenue actually saved them. And that meant that they didn't have to die. And actually, we're very quickly able to raise around that save the company. And today, the company is a massive company unicorn, etc. So I think one way to test if customers love your product is to charge them. So there's a couple other things that I think about a lot in pivots. One is, I recommend like trying to figure out as soon as possible. Usually, when you raise a seed round, you have 18 months, maybe 24 months of runway. And if you figure it out too late, if you're at the end of your runway, you know, it's going to be very difficult for you to survive and raise money. So what I like to say is, you know, within the first six months or so after launching your product, you should know if there's a strong customer pull. And if you're feeling that customer pull, it's going to be palpable. People are going to be talking about it with their friends. And you're going to get a bunch of customers that way. Like you're going to see tweets about it. investors are going to have heard about your company through their portfolio companies. So all that stuff is going to be happening. And if you're not feeling that immediately, you might need to pivot. And pivoting doesn't necessarily mean you change the business entirely from one thing to another. There are a lot of different ways to pivot. In the case of Albert, there was a small business model tweak, which was we move from a free service to a paid service. That's one type of pivot. Other companies in a similar space, like we mentioned Plaid, Plaid had built a similar product and pivoted to providing infrastructure that they had already built. So a lot of pivots are actually not wholesale changes like some of the ones we talked about earlier, but more smaller changes where you use the same product and sell to a different customer set. In fintech, it's very common for folks to start building a consumer product and realize that actually it might be better if you sell that product to banks. And banks can use that as a channel for their own customer acquisition. We see that quite frequently. So the other thing I want to talk about is, again, like this pivoting early concept. What I mentioned is like ideally in six months, you kind of know if the company, if you're, if you're feeling this market pull, if you don't feel it, it could also be that your product isn't quite there yet. Like you might have launched prematurely and that definitely happens. But what I'd encourage you to do to figure that out is talk to your customers. There's never a bad time spent talking with customers. What you should be focused on if you feel like you don't have product market fit. And even when you do is just talk to customers as much as you can and understand if they don't like your product, what is it that they don't like about your product? And if they do like your product, what would they like to see you change? And I will say it's easy to get into a paralysis from this because you might talk to 10 different customers and it's like the, like that terrible with the elephant. And like every customer tells you something different. But I do think overall, talking to customers and actually spending real time with them, having them go through your product helps you eliminate a lot of these problems and might help you understand a pivot. And sometimes a customer might say, well, I like this, but what I really need is something different. And we have a company in our portfolio that had a huge pivot. They were selling a product to hospitals and they realized after spending a bunch of time implementing with these hospitals, that the CIOs of these hospitals were actually telling them, this is great, but you know what would be even better. And they pivoted that product and now have had a lot of success and actually also went from a ACV in the tens of thousands of dollars to now an ACV annual contract value, in some cases, the millions of dollars with a single customer, truly incredible pivot. So the other thing to think about is when you do make a pivot, if it's a sharp pivot, you want to make sure that your team is on board. Like I've seen this happen. One thing we talked about was the idea of a fintech company pivoting from serving consumers to serving banks. Well, there's a big difference. And the team that helped you serve consumers may not be and probably isn't the same team that's going to help you sell into banks. Like you might have a bunch of great growth marketers that were helping you sell a product to consumers. Well, unfortunately, if you make that pivot, that team is probably less likely to be useful in your new company. As you do the pivot, I would, you know, try to first get alignment from the management team and make sure that that's what you want to do. It's actually okay to start in a small way. So you can originally do a bunch of tests. So maybe you have that consumer app going, but you test selling into banks. And if you're feeling a stronger market pull from the banks, then go in that direction and also pivot the team that way. If you do a wholesale pivot, like it's important to get buy -in from the entire team. It can be a real morale killer for somebody to feel like they weren't heard in the process. One thing I'll say on that is besides getting the team bot in, you also need to pivot how you think about the company. And so your metrics need to change. I always encourage people to have a few Nordstar metrics that they're always tracking and always talking about. So like in the case of Mercury, it might be deposits and customers. So there are a bunch of KPIs you need to track as a company. And as you execute the pivot, those KPIs also need to change. So as a team, what I would do is talk to them about the pivot. And as a team, define new benchmarks that align with the pivot. So you can measure that success of the pivot accurately. And this could still be the case while you're running the old business. If the pivot is a micro pivot while testing, you want to define what success looks like. The recap things I would say, pivot early because you have a limited runway. Within six months from launch, ideally, you have a sense on whether things are working. Use customer feedback as your Northstar. Continually talk to customers and get deep engagement with them. Don't just ask them questions. Try to actually sit next to them and talk to them, buy them a coffee. Make sure your team is aligned in the new direction. And remember, a lot of amazing companies pivoted. Pivoting can be the smartest thing you do as a company. And the final thing I'll talk about is because I'm an investor, you might wonder, well, what will our investors think? And what I'll say is investors want you to succeed. That's the most important thing. I do think it's important to talk to investors along the way. They can be a great sounding board. They might have seen other types of pivots and other types of companies doing what you're trying to do. So again, I would involve customers,

They can raise prices, increase profits, and users have no choice but to stick around. And worst case scenario, B &B Air raises $10 billion, $20 billion, $100 billion to play hardball. Airbnb can still decrease prices, cut margins, and they can keep churning away. There's no problem. Eventually, like Uber, the competitor runs out of cash and goes belly up. Game over. And I know this is controversial, but you want proof? Look at Benchmark. Benchmark Capital is one of the premier VC firms in the world, especially in the US. So why are they suing Sweetheart Uber and Travis Kalanick? Benchmark invested $12 million in Uber. That's now worth approximately $7 billion, at least at Uber's last valuation. That means Benchmark's 20 % carry. So how it works in VC, you get two things. You get 2 % management, so however much of the funds they're managing, plus a 20 % carry. So if you turn $100 million into $100 billion, you're getting 20 % of that change. That's big, big, big, big, big money. So Benchmark's 20 % carry is worth approximately $1.397 billion. That's game -changing money. That's throw away your reputation and make it rain money. At least it seems to be for Benchmark. It's also indicative of something else. Benchmark sees these challenges. Makes no mistake about it. Uber has its fair share of enemies from its meteoric rise. But I'll bet Benchmark is worried about going to zero. They're worried about crashing. Uber in its infinite playbook is starting to run dry. As of August 23, 2017, Uber's burn rate was about $2 billion per year. Uber's a forest fire that's running out of fuel. Without significant funding or, better yet, pricing power, which they can't have because there's too much competition, Uber's going to burn itself to the ground. Imagine, for all of our American fans, a running back racing towards the sidelines. They're trying to beat the defense, turn the corner. If Uber turns the corner, it's like 100 million touchdowns. Unfortunately, in a world of increasingly many and increasingly powerful competitors, there are no touchdowns. Benchmark sees the light. Either unload the stock or IPO so they can cash out. They can't let this $1.4 billion payday airliner crash. So what do they do? They need a liquidity. But let's look at the future. What about AI? What about driverless? Does that save Uber? The short answer? No. Uber's business model is predicated on drivers owning the cars. In a world of autonomous vehicles, where vehicle ownership, where does that lie? Odds are fleets or privately owned. Odds are fleets. So privately or publicly owned. That's the question. What happens for Uber's driverless cars? Well, there's a couple choices. A. Uber can buy them all or they can lease them. Those are the only two options. Either way, their costs go through the freaking roof. So they're owning them or they're leasing them from somewhere else. And don't forget about auto insurance. And probably driverless insurance. Oh, and fleet maintenance costs as well. And while autonomous vehicles increase efficiencies and reduce empty times, and they're going to cut out all of these driver fees, what happens at night? Uber's demand graft. You guys can't see the picture. I can. But if you go to the article, thesyndicate.vc, you can find it there. But if you look at their demand chart, from essentially 9 p.m. on to midnight, there's almost no... Wait, that can't be right. I think I'm looking at the times wrong. Either way, there's essentially zero demand in the dead of night, which makes sense. So what percentage of the time will cars go unused? It's definitely not zero percent. That means massive capital expenditures and waste. Suddenly, Uber's driverless cars aren't quite so sexy or profitable. What happened to the world's largest tax company that doesn't own a single car? Plus, there's another problem. Competition. Google's better when it comes to autonomous vehicles. And there's a crop of startups and corporates lining up to compete. Then there's Tesla. I would never, ever count Elon Musk out of a fight. He is a freakin' baller. The question is, can Uber overcome this? Is this a scenario where Uber... Is there a possible scenario where Uber wins? Maybe. Think outside the box. I argued in a recent post about Google's ability to be the operating system of autonomous vehicles. Could a Chrome -like platform be built for driverless cars? Capturing customer attention and creating value. The reason for this? Voice disrupts Google. What happens when their search business is gone? They need something else. Hence why they've gone hard on autonomous vehicles and a bunch of other projects they've been working on. But anyways, what about Uber? What if Uber owned a company like Netflix or Hulu? They could sell content and entertainment on the rides. Uber needs an upsell. They need a way to increase LTV and margins without added spend. And most importantly, they need a way to keep customers and drivers. Upsells via content or affiliate marketing channels could be that system. Some Uber drivers, they already do this on their own. They have some type of system to earn extra money from advertising. They have those little TV head displays. They're doing a lot of things like this. Uber needs to learn from their freaking drivers and figure out a way to make their business work. And that's the question. Could this extra income could allow Uber to cut the rates or commissions if necessary to keep drivers or riders on the platform and keep out competition? This is a completely thrown out there theory, just making it up as I go. But you know what? It seems to be interesting. It seems like something they could do. Either way, they need an upsell. What are your thoughts? Are there holes in the logic? What are you thinking? Is Uber screwed? Would you rather run Uber or Airbnb? Can Dara, the new CEO of Uber, save it from itself and its business model? These questions aren't considered enough by the tech community. Uber is arguably the greatest hit in the history of VC, at least pre -IPL. And the bigger they are, the harder they fall. And the bigger their appetite. I'm bearish on Uber. I'm incredibly bullish on Airbnb. What about you? If you enjoyed this little blog cast, I guess we can call it, if you thought this content was valuable, interesting, etc., make sure to share it around. Come over to thesyndicate.vc. You can get on our expert roundtable list. So we've had some really incredible guests on talking cryptocurrency. We had another one on AI and the future of autonomous vehicles. We've got one coming up with Tim O 'Reilly and James Allworth on consumer tech and the future of what that all looks like. It's incredibly interesting. I try to get the smartest, best, brightest people on. Thesyndicate.vc. If you put a little dashed subscribe in there, you can get on our email newsletter and get all the great stuff. And if you're an angel investor, I encourage you to join our syndicate. Thesyndicate.vc. I am your reader, writer, host, whatever you want to call me, Matt Ward. And hopefully this has made you think. Because that's my goal, to make you think. When you're thinking, you're learning. And when you're learning, you're becoming better. Because if you're not learning, you're dying. Kinda like Uber. Talk to you guys again soon. Cheers.

sources.text:
[SPEAKER_01]
Our first session in the America Zone today is a panel discussing the digital and cultural transformation in a post -COVID world. The panel is moderated by Conan French, IFF. Joining him, Dr. Lita Glyptis, Chief Client Officer at 10x Future Technologies, Matthias Kroener, founder and former chief executive of Fedor Bank, Nigel Verndon, co -founder and chief executive officer of Rails Bank, and Shil Mohat, founder at Better Tomorrow Ventures. Let's now join Conan and the panel for their discussion.

[SPEAKER_05]
Thanks very much, Glenn. And the title of the session was actually co -COVID world. And I think that that's a phrase that MD Ravi Menon and others have used to note that this isn't sort of a pandemic that we're just waiting for the post -COVID world, but that there are altered conditions that we'll be living with and working in for some time as society and financial services grapples with this new environment. So I always strive to have sessions be lively and informative. And with this group, I have no doubt that we will have a great and exciting session. So the first thing that I wanted us to really jump into is, how are financial service firms doing in the reaction to COVID? How are they doing in supporting society and its needs right now? And if you thought of this pandemic and the reactions to it as a referendum on digital transformation of the industry, what do the results look like? So Lida, maybe if we could start with you with your thoughts.

[SPEAKER_03]
It's an interesting question and one that we get asked a lot. And I must admit that I always frown a little bit when I hear representatives of financial institutions celebrating the amazing results they have had in terms of their coping and the policies they put in place. And not because they haven't, but because it's a mixed bag. So I would say that the majority of financial institutions have been ranging from pretty good to very good at coping with the immediate challenges of equipping their colleagues and their teams to deal with the immediate tasks at hand, throwing people at the challenge of creating payment holidays and sort of practical solutions, and providing bridges built with extraordinary human effort to actually deploy some immediate solace and immediate comfort. Have they been good at taking stock and making some radical bold moves down their digitization agenda? A digitization agenda that has been simmering for the last 15 years? I would certainly, I would say largely not. We have seen some extraordinary results that were the outcome of human effort, but we have also seen the limitations of the cautious digitization effort of the last few years. We have seen the gaps that not having truly digitally native capabilities give us. And we have also seen our reluctance, understandable, but also dangerous, to commit to the radical next move that would give us the infrastructure that would have made coping with the challenges a little bit easier. So how have they coped? Largely okay. Have they been able to really go out of their way to give something of a springboard to their communities? I would have say not, but they were not equipped for that.

[SPEAKER_05]
So Nigel, that same question to you, you know, making sure that things functions, making sure the sort of lights fit on, that people could work from home was sort of a herculine effort. But if we really think about a transformed world and living in conditions like this for a while, or, you know, a very different economy economy and landscape coming out of this, what are your thoughts on how the industry is done?

[SPEAKER_00]
Nigel I think, yes, everybody's put a great effort into to be able to work from home and other efforts. But I think there's a real reality slap of the billions that have been spent in the financial services industry in industry on digital transformation has really ended up in what colleagues and others call as a digital death zone. Because it's a place where analog processes have just been automated, as opposed to a true digital type of business. Now, this is an example of this. We clear sterling with the Bank of England directly, and also clear euros, we're all principal members of Visa, Moscow. We sent all our company home, and the customers didn't realise that we sent it out more than others, because we're used to dealing in a risk environment, having built companies through the dot -com bust and the credit crunch. But when the large institutions sending people home, there was definite impact to service. And that shows that there's still a lot of analog process, even in the digital channel, the apps, etc. So I think it's been a massive, massive wake -up call to actually realise that digital is not about having a digital channel. It's a mindset of removing friction from your processes, automation, etc. And if you look at Amazon, Amazon is essentially a logistics business. Google is a hardware, computer hardware business, if you look at it under the covers. And those still have the mindset of creating great digital product as frictionless to use for consumers, massively scalable, and have that ability. And just another observation is most financial institutions, only 3 % of them have any, on the boards, of people who've got a true digital background. And that's quite telling when you have to, I think, create the post of a Chief Digital Officer, because digital should be in your DNA. And I think we discussed last time the concept of we should have Chief Legacy Officer to make sure we don't do stupid things again. But this general concept that it's a DNA -led thing, and I think this, and I hope this is good for everybody, the boards and senior management of financial services firms, I think now realize, digital is a DNA thing. It's not something you create a post to do, because Google doesn't have a Chief Digital Officer, neither does Amazon, neither do we, neither do Fidel Bank, and others. I bet 10x doesn't either. So, this is the real difference. And I appeal to colleagues in the industry, let's all work together, because banks still need it, because they're sensors of safety, and run by very, very good people. People like ourselves around the table here are digital natives. I think if we actually work together, we kind of get better outcome for the person we care about, which is the consumer at the end of the day, and SMEs, and customers.

[SPEAKER_05]
Mattias, we'll dive into some of those questions that Nigel just brought up a bit later about culture, and how to drive transformation in the institution. But before we do that, I would imagine you have some thoughts on what COVID has shown on the digital transformation of the industry, and what you think the landscape looks like, how they've done so far.

[SPEAKER_04]
Conan, that is so sad, because I really wanted to follow up to Nigel with his points, and we had so much fun talking about the chief incumbent officer.

[None]
I really

[SPEAKER_04]
call for that position, and I'm sure out of some banks, we will have some applications for that. No, but joking aside, actually, I do not see any progress of incumbents becoming digital, right? As Nigel said it, and Lita said it, it's a holistic topic. It's definitely not only technology, and participating in a Zoom call doesn't make you a digital native, right? So it's about corporate culture, it's in particular about the target operating model, it's about your data management, it's about innovative technologies that we could apply in financial services from Bitcoin to smart, sorry, from blockchain to smart contracting, and so on and so forth. I would not see anything so far. I think yes, what we have to say, the incumbents definitely, and the players in the market definitely did do a very good job on their resilience in terms of emergency plans, moving out of the offices, going to home office, and so on and so forth. But in banking, that shouldn't be an issue, should it? Because in banking, we have no goods to carry with us, and maybe packages to sell to our customers. It's the money, it's wired anyhow, you know, 80 -98 % of the goods we are dealing with are technical anyhow. So what is the deal about it? We just made it, okay? And what we've realized is that what decades of consultancy actually couldn't deliver, a simple virus did. Suddenly, everybody's aware of that, everybody's talking about it, and so on and so forth. At the end of the day, we are not at the end of the day today. I think it's too early to call. And we have, yes, we see operational resilience, great. We see digital not achieved. We see some points of the backlog maybe working on, but the backlog list is still very, very long. And then we come back to banking itself. We definitely will see stress on the balance sheets. And there we could see again, did they use technology maybe for collection process and so on and so forth or not? Or do we stick with the traditional way of handling it? I think it's too early to call and we will see some maybe negative surprises.

[SPEAKER_05]
So, Shail, we're starting to see some of those results and surprises. Industry has been stressed by this cycle. The fintech sector has been stressed or in some cases accelerated by the cycle. But what's your view on how institutions have done so far?

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah. mean, I think from a fintech perspective, it's been phenomenal. It's like our portfolio companies are growing faster than ever before. The transformation from e -commerce has grown nearly 50 % year over year. So the payments associated have grown quite a bit. Branchless banking has accelerated in the US very substantially. The neobanks have done exceptionally well. You know, it's funny because I come from a more traditional background. worked in consulting, primarily serving financial institutions. At that point, we were still growing branch footprint. And now, of course, it matters less and less. And then in our insurance portfolio, it's been really phenomenal. All these startups have really been significantly benefited by COVID, you know, fortunately and unfortunately. In insurance, for example, you know, like our life insurance company, for our startup life insurance company, you don't need to go to a doctor to get a test. Like it's all done online via an app versus a traditional life insurance company, you do need to get to meet with a doctor. It's been a huge boon for us. So all in all, this has been a time that fintechs have really come in and offered a service that consumers needed during this time.

[SPEAKER_05]
Yeah. And you brought up a good point, which is that this crisis has really accelerated and amplified a lot of consumer adoption. That's something that sometimes takes years or decades to drive. And we saw it in a matter of days around the world simultaneously, which was one of the really remarkable things about this. And, you know, as we heard in the earlier session, there's been some, I think, relief in the legacy banking and financial services world and regulators and supervisors that kind of the functionality worked, the bare minimum was met, society could keep going on. And there was, I think, a huge sigh of relief. But if we really want to raise our aspirations from just supporting those minimal functions and just digitizing the legacy, you know, banks and insurers and institutions, know, what do we, Nigel, wanted to come to you and see what do we really need to thrive while serving the future needs of society and some of the things that have been revealed by this crisis?

[SPEAKER_00]
Sure. It's my soapbox subject. So, I'm ready for two hours of talking out. But one of the reasons we set up at Rails Bank is we have a firm belief that access to financial services is a human right right and not a privilege. But I'm pretty sure anybody in the financial services world pretty much thinks the same. And if you look at the people's core values. One of the key issues, though, is the cost structure of the industry, especially banking, just prevents that. Because if you've got somebody who's built absolute minimum, on living on a few dollars or so, or so, and it costs you 15 to 25 bucks a month to operate a current account, how can you bank them? It should be down at 10 cents. So, the space which my co -founder Clive and I were looking at is how do we change your cost structure? We looked at parallels in other industries. And that lovely word of deconstruct everything down to its core components, which in any way has worked in consulting probably makes a good few quid selling that type of thing. But what it fundamentally means is if you look at Apple, Apple took the music industry and deconstructed it down to a simple thing called a track and a digitized track. It's for 99 cents. And that meant that A, it was available everywhere. B, it was affordable. C, it could be reconstructed and put into new forms and then to mix it into a format that you want as a consumer and it could be wrapped around the consumer. And so you had a perfect storm because you took away the LP and the form factors and you created something that didn't have something physical. If you do that to financial services, which is essentially what we've been doing for the past four years, is the same thing. You can offer product and deconstruct it and then reconstruct some bank account from us or another provider, payments from another, cards from another, and construct product around the consumer that works for the consumer that moment in time. And so it helps, that can help, I think, move the industry forward massively. And we did an announcement today, which I won't plug at the moment, but to look at our Houston product. It is also taking inspiration from, again, what Apple did originally. They made the personal computer point and click because they deconstructed how you interact with it. They deconstructed the music industry into the track. And I think if we deconstruct and work on deconstructing the financial services industry into its absolutely core components and rebuilding them around the consumer, which is this whole embedded finance movement, we've got something that does change the world. And it does mean that people who need access to finance to get it. What it does do is put up an awful lot of challenges because it changes it from being financial services, financial company or institution centric to suddenly being customer centric, customer choice. Amazon's done this, so has eBay in their respective industries. And so that's what I think is the real challenge is, can we transform the legacy into work in a deconstructed world? Because all the products fundamentally they're offering, a current account or checking account, a payment and stuff are all exactly the same. There's nothing differentiated about them and things. So that's where we see, that's why CU is where I think the challenge, that's what we've been working on and delivering.

[SPEAKER_05]
And it sounds deceptively simple to put the customer at the center and really take a customer centric view on what the needs are when you think about products and services. But again, that can be really transformative across the institution. Shield, same question to you, what do firms need to do to thrive moving forward?

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah. I think it's really just being aware of what's coming and sort of, I'd say like, fortunately for us, our software companies tend to be younger and more nimble and able to thrive in different climates. So I think it's just keep doing what you're doing and they've done well.

[None]
Matthew,

[SPEAKER_02]
to you,

[SPEAKER_05]
what are some of those things that legacy institutions maybe should be learning from the firms and the practices that Nigel and Shield just sort of walked through?

[None]
Yeah. You know, if

[SPEAKER_05]
we aspire from just digitizing today or yesterday's bank, you know, what do they need to do?

[SPEAKER_04]
Well, you know, that buzzword really for years now is used to kind of heal everything. But I would say the problem is even deeper. You know, 35 years when I, 35 years back, I started my business career in hospitality. And actually I wanted to work at a bank those days only for one reason, because one of my professors at university, teaching me hotel administration and management that say, you need to work at the bank because the bank is the enemy. And I wanted to understand the enemy. And I wanted to know how the enemy is working, how the enemy is making a loan decision for me as a future hopeful hospitality manager. And actually I got stuck. Why? Because the bank managers those days actually came back to me and said, listen, in our organization, you are the only one with a customer centric banking thinking. Sorry. And customer centric banking was the outcome of that. But, you know, that that taught me that, OK, I came from hospitality and I'm the only one who is customer centric. So this is lesson number one. You obviously do not learn that in banking. Second, what I learned is that banks are used to take the regulator as an excuse for not being customer centric, you know, because then the bank and in the meantime, I have to say to the defense of the banking and financial services industry. Yes, sometimes this is exactly the case, you know, as a bank, you might even want to go and do something good and maybe take even more risk on your books because you think now in particular days we are living in society might need it. But believe me, next next minute, the regulator will ring your doorbell and say, listen, what are you doing there? And I think so. We have to have a look to the whole environment and and that includes the regulator as a stakeholder. And then thinking back when we founded FIDER now 10 years, more than 10 years ago, we had a what I called a strategic square on what we are operating because we as a bank, as a first step. And I think this is an exercise everybody must do did have a look to society, did identify a number of mega trends within this society and created that square out of it, which, you know, cornerstones to that was like everything will be mobile. People will do e -commerce. People will still use and massively use video games. You know, this kind of behavioral people will interact on social media platforms. And that was our cornerstone and we positioned our feeder bank concept. Well, hopefully in the middle and say, OK, these are the mega trends of society we want to work in. What kind of behavior on our customer side is to is to be expected so that we are a good partner for that? And this kind of exercise I do lack and do not see at all, because I would say the problem starts with banks not having an idea about a digital lifestyle is.

[SPEAKER_05]
Well, Lida, Matthias has mentioned some constraints that a lot of legacy institutions work under and you were responsible for innovation to large legacy institutions. And as you think about sort of that future that we've fast forwarded into this year of e -commerce, embedded finance, very distributed activities, what are some of the things that you think institutions need to do to really thrive and meet customer and society needs going forward?

[SPEAKER_03]
So I agree with everything that has been said, and I love the way in which it was said. And I feel slightly conflicted that I am always in defense of bankers. But I think there is something there is something worth flagging here. And it was said before, but let's tease it out. The the world that most legacy banks operate in is is a hybrid now because they have evolved from a time when a lot of what is now possible wasn't. And their technologies are in their state. It comes with immense complexity. Some systems still carry behaviors from a time when real time connectivity was not possible, let alone desirable. And therefore, the transition of digitizing and trying to keep the shop running while transforming comes with a lot of challenges that have been described. Have the banks been learning? Yes. Yes. Are the banks coming to the table to to talk to Fedor back in the day about white labeling their platform, to talk to Rails Bank, to talk to us at 10x about what the future needs to look like? And are they going on a journey that is hard? Yes. But is it fast enough? And I would say that the biggest realization that has come to banks in the last few years is twofold. One is the bank is no longer in control of the timing. For those of us who have been on the banking side for a very long time, we know that we felt that we had choices to make and we had the time in which to make them in a way that felt comfortable. And banks have realized, be it the virus, be it the rapid digitization of life around us, that they no longer control the timing. The second piece, Matthias already mentioned, but it's worth stressing, the regulator used to be the thing that a lot of banks hid behind. Now the regulator has a profound understanding of what is possible and the value it brings for customers and consumers. So they create accelerated pathways that say to banks, we will give you time to do what you need to, but we will no longer give you air cover. And those big realizations, it's not our tell, the timing is not in our control and the regulator expects better because they know better is possible. It's creating an accelerant for the banks. And it's not easy, but I do believe that we're getting to the point where it's inevitable.

[SPEAKER_05]
And Lita, that's a great summation of the changing environment, I think, that everyone is working in. At the IF, we spent the last year looking at sort of what was working and what wasn't working in digital transformation. Why? What were some of the internal barriers and challenges, external? And the question of culture and the environment with the regulator came up frequently. And I think culture, you know, is a big issue. It sounds a little squishy, it sounds sort of background, but when you think about the risk culture that was developed and grew up in banks and insurers for some very good reasons for a long time, that's one of the keys that we really need to work through in this transformation. And so that's a subject that I'd like to go to next, Matthias, is how do you really change the culture from a legacy product and vertical organized culture that's really set by sort of the last generation of technology and regulation? And how does the entire ecosystem sort of work together to transform that culture?

[SPEAKER_04]
Yeah, well, to start it with the outcome or the result, no way of changing that. Full stop. I would not even follow that pipe dream that you can change that. Not in my generation. You know, I'm potentially the eldest in this round, but I will not see that. So I think if you do not have a company that is driven by the CEO, backed fully by the shareholders and understands that the whole organization needs to convert into a digital organization. And again, I'm not speaking about technology only, right? I do not see any chance that you can convert that because there will be maybe some people hiding in the organization, waiting for that storm to pass. And once there is any kind of mistake or risk occurring out of that digitization, innovation centric whatsoever, process and program, they will raise their hand and say, listen, I could have told you this is all shit. This will never work. And as long as those I could have told you are part of your organization, you will not succeed on this. It's simply born to fail, first of all. Second, out of my B2B sales experience. Yeah, let us be blunt on this. You know, we do not have that much time to be kind of kind. Out of my B2B sales experience, I can tell you, you make a sales pitch, successful sales pitch in banking. If you address the potential that the decision maker on the accountable person is going to jail, then you have a successful sales pitch. OK, so you're going to go for compliance reason. You're going to go for risk management and all this. If you have a sales pitch, which is customer engagement, which is UX, maybe which is dealing with financial illiteracy, which is making the position of the customer more comfortable and so on and so forth. Everybody will say, yes, that's a great idea, but we will have no time for that. Now, COVID is eating up that little budget that was for customer experience and customer improvements and will focus all the budget for compliance and risk management topics. Because we will see negative impact on the risk related business like loans and so on and so forth. So I see this to be a big, big, big step backwards, actually, because the budget is not around. The culture is not in place. Yes, we understood how to operate more like via Zoom and from home. But that's it, guys. This is it.

[SPEAKER_05]
So Lita, how do you see the situation? Do you have a similar read?

[SPEAKER_04]
Say it. Say it.

[SPEAKER_03]
I agree. I totally agree with both the urgency and the focus of what is being said. I also agree that the softly, softly approach of let us do a little bit. It's like that feeling of I want to take as much of my space with me into the future, right? As much of the things I'm comfortable with knowing and doing. And I think that the realization that that won't work is absolutely there. And to Matthias' point, if that's how you're doing it, you're set to fail. But I do think that what you said right at the beginning about risk cultures may hold the key to this. Because for a very long time, as we said, and it's human nature, right? It's not bank bashing. People have been hiding against the reason why we most recently didn't do something. It was the regulator. was the risk and compliance department. And if you look at how a lot of our risk and compliance departments have traditionally worked, it's checklists that show that even if something has gone wrong, you did all the right things to avoid it. The mindset that you need to deliver meaningful digital capabilities is a combination and balance of the opportunity cost of not doing and of the potential permutations of risk around the possible use of technology, the possible implications. It's a completely different risk mindset. And we have never looked to the risk department as the potential driver of transformation inside a bank. But I'm going to throw it out there that the banks that manage to transform their risk function now have the highest chance of success in the next few years.

[SPEAKER_05]
And I think at the IF, one of the things that we've seen is a change, certainly at the top of house of the leading regulators and supervisors, to realize that not transforming is actually a fundamental risk to the industry. You know, we were very focused on the risk of moving to cloud until we sort of highlighted what are the risks of not being able to move and translate things into a cloud environment. So, Shiel, maybe a comment, you know, risk and compliance, if it's in the ascendancy, I think also there are a number of fintechs that became acutely aware of AML and KYC risks and operations this year. Yeah, so I think of it as, so first of all, we take a very broad definition, but I think at its core, Fintech is infrastructure to exchange resources with people that you don't necessarily know, and it could be a trusted or non -trusted party. And I think that's at the core of finance as a whole. And then where we look beyond that, and our tagline is everything is Fintech, it's because like payments, lending, insurance, we think will be embedded into a lot of companies in the future. And so an example would be, let's say Uber. So Uber, you know, everybody knows the company. Part of what it does at its core is actually a payments facilitation, right? Like you used to have to use your credit card in the taxi, but now because of Uber, you don't have to. But there are any, several more elements of it that I think make it a Fintech company, including like how they transact with their drivers. So there's, there's a payments component there, but then also there's like, you know, their driver has to sign up to get a bank account to become an Uber driver. And, you know, Uber has tossed around the idea of themselves being a bank for their drivers. [SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, for sure. I'd grown up thinking that I was going to get into tech and had a computer in front of me at a young age. I was on the internet at a young age. I was building computers when I was single digits back when you really just had to stick a few pieces together in a box. And so I always thought that I was coding and everything like that. I always thought that I was going to get into tech. But then I got to college. I went to MIT with the intention of studying computer science. And then the internet bubble burst right after I started college. I watched all the upperclassmen basically fail to get jobs. The tech companies stopped coming to the career fairs. And at the same time, I had this interest. I'd always had this interest in just money and financial markets and got seduced by Sloan, the business school there at MIT, and ended up switching from computer science to studying math and finance. Naturally, when you study math and quantitative finance at a school at MIT, I ended up on a trading floor after I graduated. And I traded interest rate derivatives at JP Morgan for about six and half years. I was a prop trader for a while there before the financial crisis happened and all the prop traders went away. And then I was on the sell side swaps desk for a little over a year after the financial crisis before deciding to just pull the ripcord and get out of there. I knew a couple of years into Wall Street that I made the wrong choice and really wanted to switch gears back to thinking more about tech. And I was taking the GMAT, taking the GRE, thinking about how am I going to get out of Wall Street? How am I going to find my way to Silicon Valley? Meanwhile, reading TechCrunch on the trading floor every day on my new iPhone and having to read about friends of mine from MIT who had gone on to start these amazing businesses, Dropbox, while I was trudging away with Salaryman on a trading floor. Early 2010, I just had enough and I left and I moved to California and didn't really know what I was going to do. My thought process at the time was just, I'm not going to figure it out on a trading floor. I don't really want to go to business school. So instead, I'm just going to move. I'm going to start building. It's going to force me to learn. It's going to force me to meet people. And then when I inevitably fail at that, at least I will have built a network and built a skill set that could help me find a job somewhere else. Maybe I could go knock on Drew's door and there's something for me at Dropbox. Who the hell knows? So that was my view. Thankfully, I had a friend, Tim, that I'd known since middle school. He's a lot smarter than me and was working on this idea for NerdWallet. I grabbed onto his coattails and rode that for a few years. And NerdWallet did quite well, thankfully, mostly thanks to Tim. After a few years when NerdWallet outgrown me and my abilities, I helped Tim hire a bunch of people to replace me and really set up the executive team for the next wave of growth. And that's when I stepped away, led to where I am today. That's when we get into the investing stuff that I think you'll really want to dig in more.

[SPEAKER_00]
started as a math major and then switched to the business side. You were a trader at a bank, then came to Silicon Valley with a blank sheet of paper. You tried to write the next chapter of your career. Then you created NerdWallet with Tim. And then after all of that, you made a bunch of angel investments as well. And now you decided to start Better Tomorrow Ventures.

[SPEAKER_01]
When I left JP Morgan and decided to work on NerdWallet with Tim, that was basically me saying, I have this vision of what I want to do in the future. But by anybody else's standards, I'm not qualified. I'm not an engineer. Nobody in the tech industry will hire me. So I'm just going to go do my own thing to learn how to be qualified. Thankfully, that became NerdWallet. When I left NerdWallet, did the same thing. I was like, I want to do investing. I don't know enough about it. No venture fund is going to hire me because I don't know any venture funds. NerdWallet never raised any venture capital. I'm just going to start angel investing and helping founders figure it out as I go and

[None]
learn

[SPEAKER_01]
as I go. I did that for a long time. My thought process there, similar to how I figured if I work on building a business, I'll learn enough about building businesses that another business will hire me. I thought that I will start angel investing and learn enough about investing that maybe I can go join a venture firm. But I didn't know if joining a venture firm was the right thing. I might decide to start a company. I might decide to join a company. I might decide to keep angel investing. I might decide to start a venture fund. I didn't know, but I figured that angel investing similarly would be that forcing function to meet a bunch of people, to learn a bunch, and then put me in the best position. I spent more than five years doing that full -time to just create as much surface area of opportunity as possible for myself. Then ultimately, along the way, I realized that angel investing is fun. I'm loving meeting founders. I'm loving helping founders. I'm loving watching these companies develop and having a front -row seat. I joke sometimes that investing in Silicon Valley is basically legal insider trading. It's pretty cool to have direct access to the executive teams and have a very small thumb on the scale in terms of helping them think about strategy and recruiting and all this other stuff. I found that much more interesting than just putting all my money into the S &P or something like that. That was the thing that I loved about it. The thing that I didn't love about it was that as an angel investor, I'm just such a tiny part of any one of these stories. Financially speaking, I'm never going to move the needle for any of these companies. Even operationally speaking, once they go on and raise much money and they have a board and stuff that I'm just such a small part of the overall trajectory, I wanted to have more impact and I wanted to have more leverage on my own time and on my own capital and just on the types of businesses that I love working with. I joined on with Shiel, my current partner, when he was building the 500 FinTech accelerator at 500 startups. Part -time helped him build that over the next few years and really enjoyed working with him, enjoyed continuing to work with his founders, but doing it in a bit of a more scaled up fashion. We raised money from outside LPs, all this other stuff. There was more accountability to all of it and a bit more of that leverage that I was looking for. But then Shiel and I decided that we wanted to keep doing that together. We just didn't want to do it at 500. So we took everything that we learned and the networks that we'd built and everything and institutionalized that into BTV. So short answer is I wanted to have more leverage and have more influence and be able to play a bigger part in the growth stories of many of these startups.

[SPEAKER_00]
How is your view at Better Tomorrow Ventures different from other FinTech firms? Do you have a different thesis, different focus?

[SPEAKER_01]
I don't know that our view is that different. I would say that at least not today. So a little bit of the history here. When we decided to start BTV, we first started talking about it back in 2017. We didn't actually pull the trigger until 2019. But back in those days, there weren't a lot of early stage funds focused on FinTech. There were a handful who were focused on FinTech, but tended to write small checks behind other leads. And then there were larger generalist funds that did not focus on FinTech. What we found with 500 FinTech and with my own angel investing was we thought that people were pouring way too much money into opportunities in the FinTech that we didn't think deserved the amount of capital they were getting. Meanwhile, the things that we thought were most interesting, it was really hard to get people to commit to because they didn't understand it. One of the prototypical examples is we backed a company out of the accelerator called Indio. You probably know quite a bit about it was SaaS workflow software for wholesale commercial insurance brokers. And you said those words to your average VC and they looked at you, you were speaking Greek. Part of our thesis when we started BTV was we need to be that early stage capital. Somebody needs to step up and lead these rounds with conviction who actually understands their business models. What set us apart and sets us apart is if you look around at a lot of the early stage funds, there aren't very many teams. And there might only be one or two where the partners have backgrounds in financial services, have built FinTech companies, and have invested in FinTech companies. And for our part, we, for years, were the most active investors in early stage FinTech. We've backed probably some 120 or 130 FinTech companies. I guess we've seen a lot of it play out. And we were there for a lot of the development of the FinTech ecosystem as a whole over the past decade. That makes us unique.

[None]
This

[SPEAKER_00]
is a really interesting time to focus on FinTech because that sector is blowing up and the trends are very, very strong. And both of you started in FinTech way before it was cool. How is FinTech different today compared to when you started looking at FinTech?

[SPEAKER_01]
Oh, man. Yeah. So I mentioned that when we were starting to put together plans for this fund, we felt like there wasn't enough capital chasing these early stage FinTech companies or supporting these early stage FinTech companies. Between the time we started raising the fund and we closed the fund, that whole idea just went right out the window. Now, FinTech has really matured, I would say. The exit pipelines have just totally blown open. IPOs of a bunch of notable companies. We've seen a bunch of, a lot of massive M &A that really kick -started these things, like Credit Karma going to Intuit, and then Plaid initially going to Visa before that got scrapped. Once we started seeing these blockbuster exits one after another, FinTech really started to heat up and then COVID hit. And COVID just accelerated everything by years. We see Stripe go to the moon, Robinhood go to the moon, you name it, Chime. Then the existing players like Square and PayPal and stuff are just having banner years. What happened was all of a sudden, everybody wakes up to the opportunity in the FinTech space and everybody starts chasing those same opportunities that we're going after. We still think there's a bunch of money chasing ideas that don't make any sense. We joke that you can write FinTech infrastructure on a napkin and somebody will give you a $5 million seed round without really understanding what it is that you do. But the fact of the matter is, it's just gotten a lot more competitive over the last year or so in the space that we play. And funny enough, it's not really the early stage capital that we're generally competing with. It's the later stage capital coming down and trying to plant their flags as early as possible, trying to get as much of that FinTech exposure as possible that we're bumping up against the most. So there's just the amount of capital has changed considerably. We also heard this morning from a friend of ours that there are probably 15 to 20

[None]
micro

[SPEAKER_01]
VC funds, single GP VC funds out there right now, trying to raise FinTech specific vehicles. So it's just a very different world than how we started out.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, a lot of things have changed and there's a lot more focus on FinTech now. And there are many interesting trends as well. New banks, infrastructure for FinTech, lending, lots of these themes. How do you split work with Shield? What are things that you focus on and how does Shield spend his time? How do you complement each other?

[SPEAKER_01]
The flippant answer and the easiest answer is that Shield is the face of BTV. You will find him on Twitter. You will find him on Clubhouse. He is very active. He has a very large following. He does three clubhouse shows a week and has invitations to do something like five more, all focused on FinTech. So God bless him. Shield gets to be the face of BTV and do all the brand building and networking. Before COVID, he was also the one that spent all of his time on an airplane traveling around the world, networking and helping us build our deal flow internationally. So he's always been the public facing side of us. Meanwhile, I'm much more of the operational side of things, keeping the wheels on the bus. I don't spend quite as much time on airplanes as he does. So generally speaking, in terms of just fund operations, like that's how we tend to split things. Deal flow wise, we've both been at this long enough that we both have quite a bit of deal flow and overlapping, but also significantly different networks in terms of where the deal flow comes from and stuff. And we kind of divide a cocker on the investment side of things.

[SPEAKER_00]
What's the best way to reach you for an entrepreneur?

[SPEAKER_01]
Probably Twitter. I'm relatively active on Twitter, not as active as Shield, but that is my, that's the only social media. I get a lot of LinkedIn messages. I don't read them. I do read all of my Twitter DMs. don't respond to all of them, but I do read them all.

[SPEAKER_00]
Do you prefer personal introduction from someone in your network or are you open to cold calls and emails, tweets? How do you respond to those?

[None]
I

[SPEAKER_01]
read it all. We get a bunch of cold emails, cold DMs. My DMs are open. So I get a bunch of cold DMs. just, just bandwidth wise, this is one of the things that people maybe misunderstand or maybe just don't fully grasp about the VC life is I get a bunch of warm intros and I also get a bunch of cold inbound. And in terms of triaging my time and triaging my various inboxes, the warm intros tend to take precedence. I do read everything though. I'm just not going to respond to all of the cold inbound stuff because I just don't have the time for that. But I have made at least one investment off of a blind outreach. It's not something that I proactively avoid doing. I read it all. just that I can't respond to it all.

[SPEAKER_00]
So there's a preference for warm introductions, but you read all the messages, although you may not respond to all of them. That's

[None]
good for entrepreneurs

[SPEAKER_00]
to know. Can we pick an example of a startup? How did you meet the entrepreneur? What was the context? What did you see in them when you first met them? What were the questions you asked them?

[SPEAKER_01]
It's a good question. Every company is different. Every relationship is different. Albert could be a good example here, which is an investment we made out of the 500 FinTech accelerator. The founder of Albert Yenon Ravid had previously built a company in the FinTech space and left that company and was working on his next idea. This was back in, I want to say, 2016, 2017. I don't remember the exact timeframe. Right around the early days of the 500 FinTech accelerator. And he wanted to start a business that was effectively a PFM. So a personal finance manager to help with budgeting and keeping track of all your accounts and stuff like that. I was really impressed with Yenon. I thought that he was very thoughtful about his approach. He had some early traction. It was a cool product, but thanks to my NerdWallet experience, I was very opposed to the PFM space as a whole and refused, basically refused to make any bets in the space. I talked to Yenon a couple of times, really liked him, but just kept coming back to, look, dude, I just, I can't do it. Can't bring myself to get comfortable with this model. And Sheil disagreed with me and Sheil made the investment anyway.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_01]
ended up doing our accelerator and has at every step of the way proved me wrong. Turns out that he was able to build an incredible team. They were able to just execute, execute, execute. They figured out a business model that was fundamentally different than any of the other PFMs that were out there. And I was not in the minority. They had a hard time raising their seed in their Series A. But once they raised that Series A, was just off to the races. And they've gone on to raise a bunch more money from top tier investors since then. I don't know exactly what they've announced, but the company is going strong. And it's funny because in the early days, right after we made the investment, I still just kept thinking to myself, this company is going to plateau at some point. Customer acquisition is going to be such a hard thing as it is with most PFMs. And that's typically how they go. They end up plateauing at some point. So I kept trying to get my co -founder to buy them. These guys are executing on product much faster than NerdWallet, but we have the marketing muscle. So we should team up. And NerdWallet hadn't quite got its feet under it in terms of M &A. So we weren't really in a position to do that. Now I like to reach out to Tim every now and then and be like, yep, you missed your shot. Albert's too big now. NerdWallet can't afford them. But also rubbing it in my own face that I could have made that investment. I didn't.

[SPEAKER_00]
This is a great story. As an investor, I watch out for why I say yes and why I say no, especially areas where I'm really familiar. I worry whether, am I saying no because of PTSD? I'm

[None]
too

[SPEAKER_00]
familiar with it and all the various possibilities for failure really scare me. Or am I saying no because of good reasons? And I always doubt myself. But looks that was similar for you as well. So what do you do now as a result? If an entrepreneur comes to you with an area that you are really familiar, would you pass it to Shield for first look? Or are you now more open -minded?

[SPEAKER_01]
We definitely try to cross -check things with each other to get that gut check and that second opinion. What I missed in this one though was just a founder with a massive chip on his shoulder, which can be a really good thing. It can be a bad thing, but it can also be a really good thing. And if I had really picked up on that and been honest with myself about what I was seeing when I was talking to Yunnan about this idea, maybe I would have come away from it a bit differently. We have seen that some of our best performing companies were the result of pivots. But if you have the right team in place and they have the right hustle, they have that right chip on their shoulders, they can really make magic happen regardless of what they end up building. I'm much more aware of that now. I don't think Galbert's the only one that I missed. It's definitely not the only one that I missed.

[SPEAKER_00]
What do you look for in entrepreneurs? What are some things that really appeal to you in addition to all the normal things that we look for?

[SPEAKER_01]
That's a very hard question to answer, I have found, because to be honest with you, and this is another thing that it's hard for a lot of founders to fully understand about the VC job. So much of this is subjective. We don't have a chart where we're scoring people on a one to a 10 based on certain personality or a certain background or whatever. That's not really how it works. The things that we tend to look for are very soft. Did you win me over to this grand vision of what you're trying to build? So much of building a startup is storytelling. And so much of building a startup is sales at the end of the day. Hiring is sales. Your initial biz dev and actual sales, getting your first customers on board is all what requires a lot of charisma and it requires a lot of passion and storytelling and all this stuff. fundraising is fundamentally a function of storytelling. You really want a founder that just wins you over to this view of the world that you maybe were not aware of before. Those are the ones where you just come away so much more impressed. Then beyond that, we're talking to founders in the fintech space. There's a good chance that we know quite a bit about the market they're going after, the customers for their product, other approaches to that same problem. We might've seen a handful of other companies that were doing something similar, at least in the same space, whatever. We generally have pretty good information and pretty good coverage of the financial services space in terms of understanding the strategy. What we want to see is that the founder knows something that we don't, or the founder has some insight into the market that's going to set them. We're not always right, obviously, but in our eyes is going to set them apart from what can quickly become a very crowded field. There has to be something about the product or the distribution or just the business model where there's some unique insight. And when we push on that and we question the assumptions and everything, we want to hear that the founder has actually thought through and mapped out the risks and has a good sense of how to go about tackling those risks. Well, I guess one of the canonical ways that I've tried to explain this in the past is you'll talk to consumer fintech is very hard. It's mostly very hard because consumers don't care about finance. Secondly, because cost of acquisition and making the unit economics work is incredibly difficult. We get pitched ideas all the time where somebody comes to us with this beautiful screenshots of what a product could look like and here's the functionality and so and so forth. Okay, but how are you going to acquire customers? What's the distribution wedge here? Oh, Facebook ads, Google ads. If that is your answer, you haven't thought about it, right? You haven't realized how hard it is. Or every time somebody comes to us and tells us that their CAC is only a dollar, but Chime's CAC is whatever, or some other PFM app or some neobank or whatever. Their CAC is X dollars, but ours is only one or $2 or $5, whatever. just tells me that you don't actually, you haven't fully thought through and you don't fully understand what you're getting into.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. As a VC, this is what I live for. I love listening to that story from an entrepreneur who describes the vision of the future. And if the world were the way they wanted it to be, how beautiful it would be. It's so nice to

[None]
hear that story.

[SPEAKER_00]
Some people are truly gifted in the art of storytelling and some others are not, but that's what I live for. So it's really nice to hear that story day in, day out with these entrepreneurs. Are there some pitfalls that entrepreneurs make when they try to tell that story to you? Is there a tip or two that you can give to entrepreneurs like, don't do that?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. Most of the advice that goes around that's like, don't do that. I don't think it comes from a very good place. There's this longstanding Twitter debate and VC Twitter about whether you should send a PDF or a doc send. And I frankly don't think it matters one way or the other. And there's other things people say don't include certain things in your deck that I don't think really matter. One of those things is don't include a potential exit slide. And I agree with that, but nobody really does that anyway. So I don't know how helpful that advice is.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. I used to see that long time ago, 10 plus years ago, but these days entrepreneurs don't know that unless they come from private equity.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. Yeah. The biggest don't do that have to do with the cold inbound that we were talking about before. It's hard to go through and read all of your LinkedIn messages or Twitter DMs or whatever. And everybody's trying to get your attention or trying to pitch you something. But half of these things are clearly just form emails where the person didn't put any thought whatsoever into who was on the receiving end. And we'll get pitched things that are just way outside of anything we would ever invest in. If you spent two seconds researching who we were, you would know that. Or don't send me an inbound pitch referring to my fund as better ventures. There is a better ventures. We are not it. There is a tomorrow ventures. We are not it. So little things like that, like spell my name right, spell my fund name right, pitch me a fintech company. Don't pitch me some random thing that's way outside of what I do. And don't message me and just say, hey, I'd like to get some of your time. Or hey, I'd like to grab coffee or jump on a call. Provide some context. Why would I just say yes to that blindly?

[None]
Don't send

[SPEAKER_00]
a calendar invite unless you were asked to.

[SPEAKER_01]
That's a new thing that's been popping up is clicking on people's calendly links and putting meetings on their calendar that they didn't sign up for.

[None]
Yeah.

[SPEAKER_00]
I want to switch to the next segment of this podcast and ask you about your community involvement. Is there a nonprofit organization you are passionate about?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So I've been close with the team at GiveWell for a long time now. met them back in my New York days when they had first left Bridgewater. And I thought the idea was really interesting. GiveWell, their whole model is basically to try to quantify to the extent possible how to have the most impact per dollar, which is something I think a lot about leverage and optionality and things like that. Just generally speaking, this appealed to me and how you take that model and apply it to philanthropy and how you and some of the underlying tenets of this are that every human life is worth the same value. So if you could spend $25 to get somebody vaccinated in sub -Saharan Africa and save a child's life, that's much more impactful than if it costs you $25,000 to do the same thing in America. I fundamentally, I really believe that. And when they first started it, was taking this whole Bridgewater approach to rational thinking and quantifying everything and applying it to philanthropy. When I left NerdWallet and was looking for things to do, I re -engaged with them and ended up joining their board, actually, as well as supporting them financially. It quickly became clear that I was not a fit for a nonprofit board, but I've stayed close to the guys ever since. And I stayed close to the team there ever since and continued to support them year in and year out. I tend to just give money to the Umbrella organization. But what they do is they go through and they evaluate other nonprofits every year and come up with, here's where we think the most impact for your dollar can go. They tend to be health -related vaccines, malaria nets, deworming treatments and stuff like that, where it's more quantifiable. One of their shortcomings is that it's hard to quantify things that have more of a longitudinal or more qualitative impact, such as education. So I also give money to other organizations that skew more towards the areas that GiveWell doesn't quite cover as well. But I've always been a big fan of GiveWell and their approach to having the maximum impact.

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, Jake, this is incredible. Thank you very much for sharing so many good stories. And the last one about the nonprofit organization. You've shared a lot of wisdom from your experience as an entrepreneur and now as a new fund manager at Better Tomorrow Ventures. Thank you very much. And I look forward to sharing your wisdom with the world.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, of course. Thank you, Gopi.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thank you for listening to The Sure Shot Entrepreneur. I hope you enjoyed listening to real -life stories about early believers supporting ambitious entrepreneurs. Please subscribe to the podcast and post a review. Your comments will help other entrepreneurs find this podcast. I look forward to catching you at the next episode.
